Une tablette qui voit vraiment les choses en grand
L'un des principaux arguments est sans doute son gigantesque écran Dynamic Amoled 2X de 14,6 pouces. Sa définition de 2960 x 1848 pixels, son taux de rafraîchissement jusqu’à 120 Hz et son excellente luminosité en font un produit idéal pour regarder des films, travailler ou simplement naviguer. Malgré ce format XXL, Samsung limite l’épaisseur à seulement 5,1 mm. Le poids de 692 g rappelle en revanche rapidement qu’il vaut mieux l’utiliser à deux mains.
Sous le capot, le processeur MediaTek Dimensity 9400+ et les 12 Go de RAM de cette version assurent une utilisation particulièrement fluide, y compris avec plusieurs logiciels ouverts ou des jeux très gourmands. Le S Pen est fourni et la tablette peut aussi profiter du mode DeX pour se rapprocher davantage d’un environnement de travail classique. Samsung promet par ailleurs sept années de suivi logiciel.
Une batterie généreuse pour accompagner son grand écran
Avec 11 600 mAh, la batterie est à la hauteur du gabarit. Lors de notre test viSer, la Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra a effectivement tenu 20 h 54 min en usage mixte. La charge à 45 W demande quant à elle 1 h 56 min pour faire le plein, avec un chargeur compatible qui n’est cependant pas fourni.
À 1169 €, elle reste bien sûr un produit premium, mais cette remise la rend bien plus accessible. L'ardoise s'allège davantage avec une offre Samsung permettant d’obtenir un remboursement allant jusqu’à 250 € sous conditions, ce qui ramène la facture à 919 € — de quoi faciliter la décision.

articles.title: Swish to raise Rs 225 Cr in funding round led by Bertelsmann India
articles.text:
Swish to raise Rs 225 Cr in funding round led by Bertelsmann India
This is the second fundraise by the quick food delivery platform this year.
Quick food delivery platform Swish is raising Rs 224.54 crore (approx $24 million) in an extended Series B round of funding led by Bertelsmann India.
This will be the second fundraise by the Bengaluru-headquartered startup this year. It had raised $38 million in March in a Series B round led by Hara Global and Bain Capital Ventures.
The board of Swish passed a special resolution to issue 4,123 Series B2 compulsory convertible preference shares at an issue price of Rs 5,44,616 each, according to regulatory filings. This development was first reported by Entrackr.
The latest round will also see participation from existing investors Bain Capital Ventures, Accel and Hara Global.
Founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja and Saran S, Swish promises food delivery in 10 minutes in a model that blends the elements of a cloud kitchen and quick commerce.
Swish targets frequent, lower-ticket occasions such as breakfast, snacks, and late-night meals, rather than traditional lunch and dinner orders.
The startup relies on a tightly controlled, vertically integrated model by owning kitchens, logistics, and its consumer app, to deliver meals within a 1-km radius in about 10 minutes. By cutting out third-party commissions, the company aims to reinvest margins into food quality and delivery speed.
At the time of its fundraise in March, Swish said it served more than 20,000 orders daily, with menus spanning quick bites and full meals. The company began with smaller use cases such as coffee and snacks before expanding into other meal categories as repeat demand grew.
Swish operates in a hyper-competitive space, competing with both quick-commerce players, including Blinkit and Zepto, as well as cloud-kitchen operators.

articles.title: Nvidia Acquires HuggingFace for $12.9B - EE Times
articles.text:
Nvidia has acquired HuggingFace for $12.9 billion. The startup, which is named after an emoji, was founded by three French entrepreneurs in 2016. It has become the go-to repository for open-source AI models, datasets, and associated software libraries.
In a press conference announcing the deal, Nvidia VP of AI software Justin Boitano was faced with many questions about the neutrality of HuggingFace’s offering.
“We’re committed to helping build this community, stewarding, and fostering this community, Boitano said. “We want to continue to work with all AI developers globally to make sure that they’ve got an open and neutral platform that interoperates with every cloud provider, every hardware company in the world.”
Nvidia believes in maintaining a healthy ecosystem of closed model providers and open models, he added, noting that open models give companies the ability to build their own domain-specific intelligence. Nvidia is by far HuggingFace’s biggest contributor.
Boitano said that it’s in Nvidia’s interests to keep HuggingFace hardware-neutral.
“The Hugging Face team has built an amazing community, […] and the only way you do that is by building the trust of the developer community and giving developers access to run the models and access the datasets from any platform in the world that they want to run it on,” he said. “We are incentivized and motivated to keep this open and neutral and ensure that developers can work wherever they want to work, accessing and connecting the best open models into and across every cloud provider, every neocloud, and into every data center and make availability on every device.”
Nvidia-specific runtimes will continue to exist alongside open-source runtimes such as vLLM and SGLang, which are open and neutral, ensuring all open models in the HuggingFace repository can be optimized for all hardware, Boitano said.
HuggingFace co-founder and CEO Clem Delangue said that the acquisition would still mean all the players in today’s ecosystem can use open-source foundations to build whatever they want.
“The vast majority of what we do is open source—open models, open datasets that are by definition neutral—everyone can take them, everyone can optimize them, everyone can fork our open source if they’re not happy about it,” he said. “Almost by definition, everything that we do is open and neutral and gives everyone the capabilities to build more.”
Delangue, who is French, shot down a suggestion that the acquisition of HuggingFace was emblematic of the difficulties of building tech giants in the EU.
“All three co-founders are French, but I was already in the U.S. when we started the company, so quite naturally, we built it with American investors,” he said. “I think it’s going to create really positive effects on the European tech ecosystem because obviously the founders are French, a big part of the team is French, and so we hope that after this acquisition, they’ll be able to reinvest quite a lot in the European tech ecosystem.”
HuggingFace will continue to support open models and open datasets from around the globe, and Delangue said he hopes to include more open models out of European labs such as Mistral in France and Black Forest Labs in Germany.
Delangue said that the HuggingFace team is excited to now have the ability to “think long-term.” Nvidia’s support will enable HuggingFace to reach its goal of 100 million builders on the platform much more quickly, he said, noting that the platform has around 18 million users today.
“We think we’re at the inflection point for HuggingFace and for open-source AI in general,” he said. “We think with the resources, with the support, with the long-term approach of Nvidia, we’ll be able to do basically what we’ve been doing for the past 10 years, meaning, supporting the open-source AI community, but to the next level at a much bigger scale, which we think is really needed for the field and for the world.”

articles.title: Im Alleingang: KI-Agent zockt Portal durch
articles.text:
Portal: KI-Agent meistert Game-Klassiker im Alleingang und kostet Entwickler Hunderte Dollar
Am 3. September 2026 hatte OpenAI mit GPT-6 Astra sein neues Spitzenmodell verfügbar gemacht. Der KI-Anbieter selbst hatte Astra in puncto Cybersicherheit im Vorfeld als „kritisch“ eingestuft und nur eine Light-Version freigegeben.
GPT-6 Astra: KI-Agent spielt autonom
Anders als bisherige Systeme soll das neue KI-Modell längere Aufgaben ohne zusätzliche Anleitung weitgehend eigenständig erledigen können. Was freilich etwa bei der Ausnutzung von Sicherheitslücken schnell gefährlich werden kann. Der Entwickler Cozyblaze hat einen auf GPT-6 Astra basierenden KI-Agenten jetzt ein kniffliges Spiel durchspielen lassen.
Eines der Ziele von OpenAI bei der Gründung vor gut zehn Jahren sei es gewesen, eine Vielzahl von Spielen mit einem einzigen Agenten zu bewältigen, so Cozyblaze via X. Er habe nicht erwartet, dass das so schnell gehe. Aber GPT-6 Astra habe Valves Spieleklassiker Portal eigenständig gemeistert.
Games spielen als frühe OpenAI-Vision
Zwar handele es sich dabei nicht um einen echten Benchmark und es gebe noch viele Probleme zu lösen. Aber, so der Entwickler, dabei zuzusehen, wie ein KI-Agent autonom durch das ganze Spiel navigiert, fühle sich an, als würde die ursprüngliche OpenAI-Vision langsam Wirklichkeit.
Bei dem Experiment kam eine modifizierte Portal-Version zum Einsatz. Das KI-Modell wurden per Model Context Protocol verbunden. Dann galt es, 3D-Räume zu erfassen, Rätsel zu verstehen, Lösungswege zu planen und die Spielfigur entsprechend zu steuern, wie Golem erklärt.
KI-Agent erhält Zeit zum Nachdenken
Dabei erhielt die KI Screenshots und Angaben zur Position der Spielfigur. Nach einer Analyse der jeweiligen Situation und dem Planen der nächsten Aktion konnte der Agent die zu erledigenden Bewegungen an das Spiel schicken. Zwischendurch wurde das Spiel angehalten, um dem KI-Agent die Möglichkeit zum „Nachdenken“ zu geben.
Dabei zeigte sich, dass die KI nicht einem festgelegten Skript folgte, sondern immer wieder neue Schritte aus dem aktuellen Zustand ableiten konnte. Dafür waren räumliches Verständnis, Timing und mehrstufige Planung vonnöten. Insgesamt nahm das Experiment 24 Stunden in Anspruch. In dem veröffentlichten Video, in dem der KI-Agent das Spiel absolviert, sind die Denkpausen herausgeschnitten worden.
API-Kosten von über 570 Dollar
Für den KI-Agententest musste Entwickler Cozyblaze gut 570 US-Dollar zahlen, wenn man bei der Berechnung die dafür notwendigen API-Kosten zugrunde legt. Der Game-Durchlauf soll über 3.300 Aufrufe von Werkzeugen erfordert haben.
Derweil ist freilich nicht ganz ausgeschlossen, dass sich der KI-Agent aus öffentlich verfügbaren Lösungsansätzen zu dem fast 20 Jahre alten Spiel bedient haben könnte. Entsprechendes Portal-Wissen könnte zudem in den Trainingsdaten von GPT-6 Astra vorhanden sein, wie Golem hinweist.

articles.title: GTA 5 tourne enfin sur Nintendo Switch, mais pas comme vous l'imaginez
articles.text:
Treize ans après sa sortie, GTA 5 fonctionne enfin nativement sur la première génération de Nintendo Switch. Cette prouesse signée par des moddeurs exige toutefois une console modifiée, un overclocking pour approcher les 30 images par seconde et d’importantes concessions graphiques.
Un véritable portage natif taillé pour 4 Go de mémoire
Pour accomplir cette prouesse, les développeurs ont adapté et recompilé le code de GTA 5 pour l’architecture ARM de la Switch. Le projet s’appuie sur la version Legacy v2699, issue de la branche PC, PS4 et Xbox One, dont le code source avait fuité en 2023.
Les moddeurs ne sont donc étonnamment pas partis de la version Xbox 360 / PS3 qui tournait avec 512 Mo de RAM. Or, faire entrer ce moteur dans les 4 Go de mémoire unifiée de la Switch (dont une partie est réservée à l’OS) est une prouesse d’optimisation mémoire. Ils ont donc dû fortement compresser les ressources du jeu, tout en réduisant la distance d’affichage et la complexité des effets visuels, notamment la fumée, les explosions et les débris. Malgré ces sacrifices, Los Santos reste reconnaissable et le monde ouvert peut être exploré au-delà des premières missions.
- L'écran bien évidemment magnifique et confortable pour les yeux
- Le système de ventilation plus silencieux
- Une console qui chauffe moins
Une Switch jailbreakée et overclockée obligatoire
La démonstration relayée par Tom’s Hardware US a été réalisée sur une Switch OLED modifiée, mais sans ajout de mémoire vive. Aux fréquences d’horloge de base de la console, GTA 5 oscille entre 10 et 25 images par seconde. Un overclocking modéré du processeur, du circuit graphique et de la mémoire permet d'atteindre les 30 images par seconde dans les scènes les moins chargées. L’arrivée de nombreux personnages ou une explosion suffit toutefois à provoquer de sérieuses chutes de performances.
L’installation reste tout aussi éloignée du grand public. La version complète occupe environ 49 Go et réclame une Switch jailbreakée sous firmware personnalisé. Il faut également convertir les ressources de la version PC, appliquer des fichiers de configuration modifiés, construire un paquet exécutable et respecter une arborescence précise.
À cela s’ajoute une situation juridique particulièrement fragile puisque le projet repose sur du code source dérobé et diffusé sans l’accord de Rockstar Games. GTA 5 n’est donc toujours pas officiellement disponible sur Switch. Encore moins GTA 6…

articles.title: New-Glenn-Explosion fast 1.700 Kilometer weit vernehmbar
articles.text:
Stark wie Tschernobyl-Explosion: So weit war der Knall der Blue-Origin-Rakete zu hören
Am 29. Mai 2026 war es bei einem Test der Blue-Origin-Rakete New Glenn auf dem Weltraumbahnhof Cape Canaveral in Florida zu einer großen Explosion gekommen. Zum Glück wurde dabei kein Mensch verletzt. Es kam aber zu schweren Schäden an der Startrampe.
Infraschallwellen bis Texas zu vernehmen
Der Knall der durch die Explosion ausgelösten Schockwelle soll laut lokalen Medienberichten bis zu 217 Kilometer weit zu hören gewesen sein. Das sei aber nur die Spitze des Eisbergs, was den dabei produzierten Sound angeht, wie Live Science schreibt.
Einer Studie von Wissenschaftler:innen der militärischen US-Forschungs- und Entwicklungseinrichtung Sandia zufolge haben sich die Infraschallwellen knapp 1.700 Kilometer weit ausgebreitet. Mindestens 36 der über die USA verteilten Sensoren haben entsprechende Töne wahrgenommen, darunter eine im Norden des US-Bundesstaats Texas. Infraschall ist für das menschliche Ohr nicht wahrnehmbar.
Explosion stärker als jene in Tschernobyl
Aufgrund der gemessenen Frequenzen und der Ausbreitung der Schallwellen gehen die Forscher:innen davon aus, dass die Explosion eine Sprengkraft von 0,131 Kilotonnen hatte. Das soll die Sprengkraft der ersten Explosion am Kernreaktor von Tschernobyl im Jahr 1986 sogar noch übertroffen haben.
Darüber hinaus hat das Sandia-Forschungsteam herausgefunden, das bei der ersten Explosion nur zwischen drei und sechs Prozent des vorhandenen Raketentreibstoffs verbraucht wurden. Der Rest dürfte im Feuerball und der Rauchsäule nach und nach verbrannt sein.
Infraschall als Analysetool bei Explosionen
Die Forscher:innen zeigten sich im Rahmen ihrer Studie davon überzeugt, dass Infraschall ein bisher wenig genutztes, aber potenziell vielversprechendes Tool bei der Analyse großer Explosionen wie jener von Raketen sein könne. Die Analyse von Infraschallwellen hatte das Team zuvor schon bei der Verfolgung von Meteoren und Raumfahrzeugen beim Eintritt in die Erdatmosphäre eingesetzt.
Beobachter:innen gehen übrigens davon aus, dass die New-Glenn-Explosion eine der größten Explosionen darstellt, die man bisher im Vorfeld eines Raketenstarts registriert hat. Laut Ars Technica könnte sich allein die Reparatur der dabei zerstörten Startrampe mindestens ein Jahr hinziehen.
Blue Origin: Explosion gefährdet Mondpläne
Das betrifft auch die Nasa-Pläne zur Errichtung einer Mondbasis, die dadurch ins Wanken geraten könnten. Um die entsprechenden Komponenten zum Erdtrabanten zu transportieren, ist die US-Raumfahrtbehörde auf New Glenn angewiesen.

articles.title: 'It was absolutely necessary to build that new foundation to work from' — Creative Assembly says Total War 40k's new Warcore engine enabled it to improve 'almost everything,' from rendering and animations to handling 'the sheer volume of projectiles'
articles.text:
Creative Assembly says its new Warcore engine has allowed it to take Total War: Warhammer 40,000 into space and build 'a bigger play area for all the planets, all the solar systems, the whole galaxy — 'I think that's the biggest thing for campaign'
New and improved
- Creative Assembly says Total War: Warhammer 40,000's new Warcore engine improves almost every aspect of the game
- From rendering and animation to "the sheer volume of projectiles" that can be handled on screen at once
- The studio says the scale has been upgraded, creating "a bigger play area for all the planets, all the solar systems, the whole galaxy"
Creative Assembly has shared just how much its new Warcore engine has enabled it to improve almost every aspect of Total War: Warhammer 40,000.
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming at Gamescom 2026, lead designer Joy Dey and battle product owner Dave Petry discussed the upcoming strategy game and offered insight into how the updated Warcore engine delivers a bigger and better scale than previous Total War games.
"One thing the engine has allowed us to do is take the Total War into space, because we now need a bigger play area for all the planets, all the solar systems, the whole galaxy, really," Dey said. "And I think that's the biggest, biggest thing for the campaign."
Petry added that the engine has also let the studio easily manipulate assets in the game's 3D space and improve other features like rendering and animations, explaining that it was a "required engineering" for the team's vision.
"The rendering of things, being able to improve how we render things and the quality that we are rendering things at, the animation system, our ability to sort of build modular animations in a more modern way, and the retooling of all of that, so that we can build faster and better," Petry said.
"Just frankly, almost everything, and just in how we build and how we tool to be able to make our games a higher quality and at a better rate, right?"
The battle system also sounds amazing, with Petry mentioning the game's Havoc system and saying the engine manages to deal with physical explosions "much better" when it comes to destroying the environment, as well as the number of projectiles on screen.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"So you know, being able to bring in these these tools to be able to solve these new problems that get brought up by these really awesome games is something that we felt we absolutely had to do," he continued, "and it extends to model changes, like being able to just handle the sheer volume of projectiles that we are now spitting out of seemingly absolutely every orifice when it comes to this game.
Petry added, "It was just absolutely necessary to build that new foundation to work from."
Total War: Warhammer 40,000 launches sometime in 2027 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, Series S, and PC.

articles.title: Ventilation sans ventilateur, écran extensible : Lenovo dévoile de futures pépites pour les pros
articles.text:
Avec Acer et quelques autres, Lenovo fait partie des constructeurs ayant été les plus actifs en cet IFA 2026. Outre les modèles RTX Spark et IdeaPad annoncés, la marque a également pris soin de présenter deux concepts particulièrement intéressants, destinés à l'avenir du segment professionnel.
Nous vous parlions il y a quelques jours des modèles RTX Spark détaillés cette fois avec plus d'entrain par Lenovo, mais aussi du petit IdeaPad Vibe. Nous vous avions également présenté les nouveaux modèles LOQ dévoilés par la marque chinoise peu avant l'ouverture de l'IFA. Il nous reste maintenant à vous parler de ses nouveaux modèles ThinkBook pour faire le tour des principales nouveautés dévoilées par Lenovo à Berlin.
ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 / ThinkBook 14 Gen 9 : de la couleur pour les pros… ou un Snapdragon X2 Plus
On peut commencer avec le ThinkBook 14x Gen 2. Avec ce modèle, Lenovo vise les pros en quête d'un ultraportable très léger et facile à manipuler… mais aussi avides d'un peu de couleur sur un marché professionnel où les appareils sont souvent trop grisâtres. Décliné en Luna Grey, Celestial White, Mystic Violet et Veil Blue, l'engin mise sur un châssis de 12,9 mm d'épaisseur pour seulement 990 grammes.
On y retrouve jusqu'à un écran OLED 2,8K et 120 Hz de 14 pouces, couplé à des processeurs Intel Wildcat Lake (Core 7 de série 3 au maximum). Ces derniers intègrent dans le cas présent jusqu'à 32 Go de LPDDR5X et s'épaulent d'un maximum de 2 To de SSD. L'alimentation est quant à elle assurée par une batterie de 65 Wh sur les meilleures configurations.
Le ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 est annoncé en France à compter de 1079 euros, pour un lancement plus tard en septembre.
Attendu sur la même période, cette fois à partir de 1099 euros, le ThinkBook 14 Gen 9 est globalement moins appétissant. Son châssis est plus lourd et plus épais (17,9 mm d'épaisseur pour 1,3 kg), son écran limité à une dalle LCD IPS de 14 pouces couvrant seulement le spectre de couleurs NTSC, et sa batterie s'avère plus petite (50 Wh).
On y retrouve en revanche des puces Snapdragon X2 Plus encore rares sur le marché, ainsi qu'une webcam 5 Mpx de meilleure qualité et une connectivité Wi-Fi 7 qui fait défaut à son cousin le ThinkBook 14x Gen 2. On y trouve également un second emplacement pour SSD, permettant l'ajout d'une barrette M.2 supplémentaire en cas de besoin. Ses connectiques sont par ailleurs un peu plus étoffées, avec notamment la présence d'un lecteur de cartes SD.
Project AeroBlade : la dissipation active… mais sans ventilateur au service d'un PC hyper fin
Nettement plus intéressant, le Project AeroBlade n'est pour l'heure, et comme son nom l'indique, qu'un concept. Un concept toutefois relativement avancé que Lenovo semble projeter pour une commercialisation l'année prochaine… vraisemblablement sous une forme un peu différente.
L'appareil prend quoi qu'il en soit la forme d'un PC portable de 14 pouces. Son châssis en alliage de magnésium et d'aluminium mesure seulement 9,95 mm d'épaisseur pour 830 grammes. Il s'agit donc, à ce stade, d'un des modèles les plus fins et légers du marché, mais ce n'est pas vraiment sa caractéristique la plus intéressante.
Et pour cause, ce modèle développé en partenariat avec Intel a pour principale particularité d'embarquer un système de dissipation actif, pourtant dépourvu de ventilateurs. Avec la technologie Active Flow (conçue pour sa part avec Frore Systems), Lenovo parvient en effet à « remplacer le système de refroidissement traditionnel par ventilateur, par une architecture de refroidissement actif à semi-conducteurs ». Derrière cette technologie se cache une ventilation sans ventilateur ni pièce mécanique mobile, reposant en réalité sur deux modules hyper fins.
Ces derniers sont positionnés à l'emplacement habituel des ventilateurs. Ils intègrent des membranes ultrasoniques envoyant de l'air sous pression pour refroidir le PC. Cette technologie, assez révolutionnaire, pourrait à terme faire son entrée sur des modèles grand public pour éviter l'encrassement de nos PC portables (les ventilateurs finissant toujours par accumuler de la poussière), tout en réduisant le bruit émis par leur système de refroidissement et l'épaisseur requise par les dispositifs actuels. Ces modules Active Flow mesurent en effet moins de 3 mm d'épaisseur.
Project Swan : Lenovo nous refait le coup de l'écran OLED étirable
Ce Project Swan permet en effet à un ultraportable de 14 pouces d'agrandir son écran pour passer à une dalle de 17 pouces au format 16:9 une fois totalement déplié. Le concept en question conserve néanmoins un châssis relativement fin et léger, de 17,9 mm d'épaisseur pour 1,6 kg.
Pour l'instant, aucune date de lancement ou prix ne sont communiqués pour ces projets AeroBlade et Swan, qui font surtout office de preuve de concept et de vitrine technologique pour Lenovo.
La firme nous a néanmoins habitués à réemployer, sur certains appareils grand public, des technologies utilisées par le passé sur d'anciens concepts. C'était par exemple le cas pour l'écran déroulant du ThinkBook Plus Gen 6 Rollable, testé récemment par nos soins. Nous ne serions donc pas surpris de voir le système Active Flow ou le principe d'écran étirable horizontalement débarquer sur des PC portables Lenovo à moyen terme.
Source : CP Lenovo / Annonces IFA

articles.title: RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro : on a pris en main le premier smartphone durci à caméra d'action détachable
articles.text:
À l’IFA 2026, il n’y avait pas que le Xiaomi 18 Fold à découvrir, mais de nombreux stands avec des smartphones ou des accessoires pour le moins originaux. Celui de RugOne a retenu mon attention avec son smartphone durci dont le module photo se détache littéralement du dos de l’appareil. Cette dernière vient une véritable petite caméra d’action autonome.
J’ai pu prendre en main le RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro et essayer quelques-unes de ses promesses. Voici ce que ça donne.
Un cube magnétique qui se détache pour filmer autrement
Au lieu de trimballer un smartphone durci et une action cam séparée dans son sac, RugOne fusionne les deux. Sur le dos du Xsnap 7 Pro se clipse un petit module de 39 grammes, maintenu par un double système de verrouillage (aimant plus loquet mécanique) censé l’empêcher de sauter au moindre choc.
Une fois détaché, ce cube embarque son propre processeur d’image et communique en sans-fil avec le téléphone, jusqu’à 50 mètres de distance selon la fiche technique. La connexion s’est faite en quelques secondes à peine via une application dédiée, et non via l’application photo, qui permet d’afficher en direct l’image sur l’écran de son smartphone. Je n’ai pas pu tester la portée maximale annoncée dans les conditions du salon.
Techniquement, le module filme en 2,7K à 30 images par seconde, avec un champ de vision de 133 degrés, une autonomie annoncée d’environ 40 minutes en solo, et 64 Go de stockage embarqué. Étanche jusqu’à 5 mètres sans caisson supplémentaire, il intègre aussi une stabilisation logicielle et un verrouillage d’horizon à 360 degrés. Une fois reclipsé, il se recharge automatiquement via les connecteurs pogo du téléphone, sur la batterie de 9300 mAh du Xsnap 7 Pro.
Sur la comparaison avec de vraies action cams, il n’y a pas vraiment photo et ce n’est pas une surprise. En 2,7K, le module reste loin derrière les meilleures caméras d’action du marché, qui filment en 4K avec une stabilisation nettement plus aboutie. L’intérêt du Xsnap 7 Pro n’est donc pas là, mais bien dans cette logique tout-en-un qui évite de multiplier les appareils dans son sac.
Attention, smartphone (très) très lourd
Venu sur le stand pour découvrir la caméra détachable, je retiens aussi de cette rapide prise en main le poids et la sensation de l’appareil entre les mains. En effet, ce téléphone pèse 477 grammes. En comparaison, un iPhone 17 Pro Max tourne autour de 230 grammes. Une fois soupesé sur le stand, difficile de ne pas y penser en termes de parpaing plutôt que de smartphone.
Un « surpoids » pleinement assumé par le Xsnap 7 Pro qui propose une étanchéité IP68/IP69K, une certification MIL-STD-810H et une résistance aux chutes de 1,5 mètre sur béton, immersion de 2 mètres pendant 30 minutes.
Reste qu’on a quand même l’impression qu’il pourrait presque autant servir à filmer une randonnée qu’à caler une porte, voire à se défendre en cas de mauvaise rencontre en pleine nature.
Une fiche technique honnête, sans plus
Sous le capot, le Xsnap 7 Pro embarque un MediaTek Dimensity 8400, accompagné de 12 Go de RAM et 512 Go de stockage. Une configuration solide sur le papier, même s’il s’agit d’une puce sortie en 2025 qui officie à présent dans des smartphones beaucoup plus abordables. À l’avant, on a droit à un écran AMOLED de 6,67 pouces qui affiche une définition de 1,5K à 120 Hz, protégé par du verre Gorilla Victus.
Côté photo (sans le module détachable), on trouve un capteur principal de 50 mégapixels avec stabilisation optique et une caméra infrarouge de 64 mégapixels dédiée à la vision nocturne. La partie logicielle repose sur Android 16, avec trois mises à jour majeures promises, jusqu’à Android 20.
Un Kickstarter, donc un vrai pari
RugOne a choisi le financement participatif pour commercialiser son Xsnap 7 Pro.
Les ventes anticipées s’ouvrent sur Kickstarter le 7 septembre, à partir de 799 euros. Une formule qui implique, comme pour tout projet en crowdfunding, une part de risque assumée par l’acheteur : pas de garantie ferme sur les délais de livraison, ni sur la conformité totale du produit final par rapport aux promesses actuelles. La sortie mondiale « classique », via Amazon et la boutique en ligne de RugOne, est annoncée pour octobre, à un tarif nettement plus élevé de 1 099,99 euros en Europe, soit 300 euros de plus que le prix early-bird.
Ce tarif de lancement définitif interroge un peu au vu de la fiche technique : pour plus de 1 000 euros, la concurrence propose des smartphones dotés de puces bien plus récentes et performantes. Le vrai argument de vente du Xsnap 7 Pro reste donc sa proposition unique, ce module caméra détachable, pas ses performances brutes.

articles.text:
Monday, September 7th 2026
	
	
	
	
League of Legends MMO Still in Development Despite 2XKO's Ill Fate
It's no secret that Riot Games has been working on an MMO set in the League of Legends universe, but there have been questions surrounding the fate of that game, given the poor performance and subsequent cessation of development of 2XKO, its League of Legends-flavored tag-team fighting game. In a new panel at PAX West, Riot Games co-founder, Marc Merrill, addressed a fan question about the future of the League MMO, shedding light on its future. 
Merrill basically confirmed that the game is still in development, but his comments also suggest that it hasn't been the easiest genre to develop. "We know what players' hopes and dreams are, and it's on us as a team: Can we exceed in the execution, you know?" He goes on to suggest that the MMO is "the Holy Grail," and that it may be a difficult path, but that "the future's incredibly bright." The YouTube video with the full panel appearance at PAX is embedded below.

articles.title: Edifier ES850NB headphones review: great value option
articles.text:
After my review of their V80 headphones, Edifier was kind enough to send me a pair of their ES850NB headphones to try out. Because I love the V80s, I was excited to give these new and improved headphones a test run. I’ve been using them pretty regularly for several months, and I have quite a few thoughts.
I mentioned in my review of the V80s that my budget is limited, so price is often one of the first things I check for, whether I’ve paid for a product or received it as a gift. The Edifier ES850NB headphones are available on Edifier’s website for $199.99. At the time of writing, they’re on sale for $129.99 on Amazon Canada.
That’s a pretty substantial price jump from the affordable V80 headphones, which are regularly $69.99, and currently on sale for $39.99 on Edifier’s website and on Amazon Canada. In theory, that should mean that the difference in quality is also substantial, if the pricing is to be considered fair. However, I’m not sure that’s quite the case for the ES850NB headphones.
Don’t get me wrong: they’re excellent, and improvements were definitely made. Out of the box, the audio quality is noticeably stronger than the V80 headphones. Where the V80s required a little bit of EQ to get them sounding full and smooth, the ES850NBs can get away with the default audio settings in the EdifierConneX companion app. If you’re picky, you may find the bottom end just slightly lacking, but it wasn’t enough to bother me. I think the average listener would be more than satisfied with the overall sound.
The ES850NB’s Active Noise Cancelling (ANC) has not improved much from that of the V80 headphones. The product details of the ES850NB headphones cite -45dB noise cancellation, where the V80 headphones do -44dB. A difference of one decibel isn’t really detectable to the human ear, but I think Edifier’s use of Passive Noise Cancelling (PNC) makes a huge difference.
While ANC uses tiny microphones in a process called “phase cancellation” to monitor external noise and generate inverted sound waves to cancel out the noise, PNC refers to the use of physical design to minimize external noise interruption. The shape of headphone cups, the density of ear cushions, and the angle at which they sit over the ear are all a part of Passive Noise Cancellation.
With any headphones or earbuds, I like to test noise cancelling in a noisy, crowded environment. The V80 headphones did an impressive job with external noise suppression. It was easy to drown out the chaos and lock in, even at my favourite coffee shop during the lunch rush.
Even though the ANC on the ES850NBs is only one decibel greater than the V80s, it felt a lot stronger because they have better PNC. In addition to the external noise suppression being improved, it also effectively eliminated the sound leakage I noticed with the V80s.
I won’t pretend to know exactly how the ES850NBs reduced sound leakage – physics as a whole is mostly a mystery to me – but the headphones leak a lot less sound than the V80s. I was able to turn the volume up to almost 90% before my partner could hear what I was listening to.
This is great news if you like to listen on the louder side, but you should always be mindful of how loud and how long you listen, unless you’re cool with damaging your hearing.
The physical design of the ES850NB headphones is quite different from the V80s. The ear cups are slightly less oblong. They have gently rounded corners, creating a shape closer to a “squoval”. The cups protrude more abruptly and have much sharper edges than the round design of the V80 headphones. I don’t notice much of a difference in the density of the ear cushions or headband, but the shape of the ear cushions also leans a bit more square than oval.
Aesthetically, the ES850NB headphones are gorgeous. I have them in brown, which feels very luxurious, especially with the faux leather face on the outside of the cups. I was secretly hoping for pink, but even the brown could pass for a deep mauve. They go with everything, and they’re extremely comfortable. They are a bit warm, but I think that’s the case for just about all over-the-ear headphones.
The ES850NB headphones come with a pretty nice travel case, which is handy for keeping your headphones in great condition. I’m never a fan of tossing any device into a bag without some kind of protection, so I appreciate this addition.
The button setup is the same as on the V80 headphones, and the buttons are also customizable through the EdifierConneX app. The ES850NB headphones have a similar Bluetooth range of about 30 feet, and they also sport the same 40mm driver as the V80 headphones. The two also share the same listening modes: High Noise Cancellation, Medium Noise Cancellation, Ambient Sound, and Wind Reduction.
Edifier has added support for the LDAC codec to the ES850NB headphones, which basically allows more audio information to pass through the wireless Bluetooth connection, resulting in higher-resolution audio for the listener. It’s worth noting that device compatibility with the LDAC codec is still pretty limited. Most mid-range and flagship Android phones from 2024 and newer support LDAC, but it still varies by brand and model. Currently, there are no iPhone models with LDAC support.
The ES850NB headphones have gained an interesting new feature called Touch-to-Chat. When using ANC, you can touch and hold the right ear cup to pause playback and switch to ambient sound mode, then release to resume playback. The idea is that if someone is trying to speak to you while you’re listening to something, this will be a seamless way to have a quick chat, then go back to listening.
I really like this idea, but you have to hold for about two seconds before playback pauses. That two-second delay is just a little too long for it to be considered seamless. I find it easier to just move the cup off my ear and then hit the pause button. Touch-to-Chat is a great idea, and that delay is the only drawback for me.
Other than physical design, the biggest difference between the V80 and ES850NB headphones is the battery capacity. The ES850NBs offer a massive 53 listening hours with ANC, and 92 hours without. This is a huge jump from the V80s’ respective 26 hours with ANC and 45 hours without. You still can’t charge while listening, but the Fast Charging makes up for that fact. 15 minutes of charging will get you 11.5 hours of playback without ANC on the ES850NB headphones, versus the V80’s 8 hours.
So after all this, the question remains: “Do the ES850NB headphones live up to their elevated price point?” My answer is ultimately… kind of. Yes, they are awesome headphones. Yes, I thoroughly enjoy using them. However, I don’t feel compelled to spend $129.99 on them when the V80 headphones can do an excellent job for much less.
I think if you’re in a tax bracket where $129.99 isn’t that expensive to you, you really don’t want to bother with equalizing your headphones at all, and sound leakage will be a big problem for you, then the ES850NB headphones are a great option; perhaps even the perfect option. After all, as far as high-quality headphones go, $129.99 is still quite inexpensive.
Otherwise, I would probably advise sticking with the V80 headphones. Edifier may have shot themselves in the foot by making their budget headphones too good. In this economy, I actually think that’s something to be proud of. I’m always in favour of whatever is most accessible to the average person. A company with high-quality products at reasonable prices is a company I feel like I can trust, which is why Edifier will still be one of the first brands I look to for headphones.

articles.title: Why Microcooling Will Be a Critical Enabler of Agentic AI- EE Times
articles.text:
The AI industry is obsessed with compute. Every new generation of hardware promises more power, larger models, more parameters, and increasingly capable AI experiences. But as agentic AI moves from the cloud to billions of edge devices, compute may no longer be the industry’s most important constraint.
Thermals may be.
The prevailing vision for agentic AI depends on smartphones, wearables, AI glasses, robots, and other edge devices continuously perceiving their environment, maintaining context, and taking action in real time. That requires AI systems that can sustain performance for hours, not simply deliver impressive benchmark scores for seconds.
As a result, the future of agentic AI will be shaped not only by advances in models and processors, but also by the industry’s ability to manage heat within increasingly compact devices. In a hybrid edge-cloud world, thermal management is becoming a foundational layer of the AI stack.
The move to hybrid means thermal challenges
The largest platform providers have all arrived at a similar conclusion regarding agentic AI architecture. Qualcomm argues that AI inference should be distributed across cloud and edge devices, with local models handling immediate perception and cloud models providing deeper reasoning. Apple has adopted an on-device-first architecture that escalates only more complex requests to Private Cloud Compute.
Google follows a similar strategy through Gemini Nano running locally alongside larger cloud-based models. Even Meta’s vision for AI glasses relies on local sensing while offloading heavier inference to paired devices and cloud infrastructure.
Although these companies have different business models, they’ve converged on the same basic model: An AI agent replaces the mobile app as a primary interface, and meaningful intelligence must increasingly execute at the edge.
And unlike traditional mobile apps that perform short, discrete tasks, AI agents operate continuously. They observe their environment, maintain context, reason about incoming information, and execute actions in real time. That persistent activity alters the thermal profile of smartphones, AI glasses, watches, drones, robots, and other edge devices.
Therefore, devices need reimagining.
Agentic AI changes the duty cycle
Smartphones, for instance, have been designed around what engineers often describe as a “race-to-idle” model. A processor performs an intensive task, returns to a low-power state, and dissipates accumulated heat before the next burst of activity.
Agentic AI disrupts this model. The personal AI agent continuously monitors speech, cameras, location, sensors, and application context while periodically executing language model inference, computer vision, and planning algorithms. Instead of short bursts of computation, the workload is persistent. Therefore, sustained power dissipation, not instantaneous performance, becomes the primary engineering constraint.
This distinction is important because modern processors are already capable. Today’s mobile neural processing units (NPUs) advertise impressive AI performance measured in trillions of operations per second (TOPS), but those peak numbers matter only briefly. Once thermal limits are reached, clock frequencies fall, inference slows, and AI responsiveness degrades through thermal throttling.
For agentic AI, maintaining sustained performance matters far more than benchmark scores. Thus, the importance of thermal management.
Edge devices have little thermal headroom
Running AI locally improves latency, privacy, reliability, and operating costs. However, edge devices have constrained thermal envelopes.
A smartphone can typically sustain only a few watts of continuous power before temperatures affect performance and comfort. AI glasses operate within an even tighter power budget, while maintaining skin-contact temperatures below roughly 43°C to 45°C for comfortable wear.
These limitations become more problematic as new AI devices process multiple sensor streams simultaneously. Consider an AI-enabled pair of smart glasses. At any given moment, the device may capture video, process audio, monitor head movement, track location, maintain wireless connectivity, render displays, and execute AI inference. Each operation generates heat, yet the entire system must remain lightweight, comfortable, and nearly silent.
The smartphone industry has adopted sophisticated passive thermal technologies to deal with heat. Vapor chambers, graphite heat spreaders, advanced packaging, and optimized component placement all help distribute heat more effectively across a device. These technologies remain essential, but they redistribute heat rather than remove it.
As agentic AI shifts workloads from intermittent bursts toward continuous operation, heat redistribution alone can’t provide sufficient thermal margin. Maintaining sustained AI performance requires new approaches to localized heat removal. That is particularly true for wearables, where size and comfort restrict traditional cooling options.
Active microcooling changes the design space
Microcooling technologies offer a solution. Instead of relying on miniature rotary fans, MEMS-based piezoelectric actuators are fabricated in silicon to generate airflow inside an extremely compact package. The result—a fan on a chip—is precise active cooling that fits where conventional solutions cannot.
Localized active airflow can reduce temperatures at processor hotspots, allowing AI accelerators to sustain higher performance before thermal throttling occurs. That additional thermal headroom enables longer inference sessions, greater processor utilization, and potentially higher sustained power budgets without increasing overall device dimensions.
In addition to making small devices cooler, microcooling expands the available compute envelope. For smartphones, this can improve sustained AI responsiveness during continuous inference. For AI glasses, where every cubic millimeter and every gram matter, microcooling may enable more perception workloads to execute directly on the device instead of immediately being offloaded elsewhere.
Cooling becomes part of the AI stack
As the industry races to build more powerful AI models and faster processors, it’s easy to overlook the physical realities that ultimately determine what users experience. AI capability increasingly depends on how much compute a device can sustain, not simply how much it can deliver at peak performance.
This makes thermal management a critical enabler of AI innovation and adoption. The companies that unlock the next generation of agentic experiences will combine smarter models and faster NPUs with devices capable of running them continuously, efficiently, and comfortably in the real world.
In the age of agentic AI, the future of intelligence may be determined as much by cooling as by computing.

articles.title: Bill Gates proyecta un futuro con IA accesible para todos pero advierte sobre los peligros del cambio tecnológico
articles.text:
Bill Gates proyecta un futuro con IA accesible para todos, aunque advierte sobre los peligros del cambio tecnológico que se avecina. El cofundador de Microsoft expuso su visión en dos apariciones públicas recientes: el programa de Jimmy Fallon y una charla posterior en Harvard, donde delineó un escenario en el que la tecnología redefinirá profesiones enteras en la próxima década.
Qué dijo Bill Gates sobre el futuro de la inteligencia artificial
Durante su paso por el programa de Jimmy Fallon, Gates afirmó: “Dentro de 10 años, la mayoría de las tareas humanas podrán ser realizadas por inteligencia artificial”. La frase resume el núcleo de su pensamiento sobre el rumbo de la tecnología en el corto plazo.
PUBLICIDAD
En Harvard, ante Arthur Brooks, profundizó esa idea con un contraste histórico. “La inteligencia será completamente libre. ¿Qué significa esto? La computación antes era para hacer que las tareas existentes sean más eficientes, pero la IA podrá fundamentalmente redefinir las tareas y delegarlas en personas o máquinas”, explicó.
Brooks le señaló durante ese intercambio: “En el fondo, tu camino al éxito fue más de relaciones que de tecnología”, una observación que puso en perspectiva el propio recorrido de Gates dentro de la industria que ayudó a construir.
PUBLICIDAD
La comparación que traza Gates con su propia trayectoria resulta directa. Así como en los años 80 impulsó la idea de tener un ordenador en cada escritorio, hoy anticipa una inteligencia artificial omnipresente, gratuita e invisible, con capacidad para transformar cada esfera de la vida humana.
Cómo cambiará la inteligencia artificial la medicina y la educación
Gates identifica dos campos donde el impacto ya resulta perceptible: la medicina y la educación. Sobre el primero, sostuvo en Harvard: “Es algo muy profundo y un poco aterrador.
PUBLICIDAD
Porque está sucediendo muy rápido y no hay un límite. Una de las transformaciones más grandes es en diagnósticos médicos. Con el tiempo, las máquinas probablemente sean superiores a los humanos porque la amplitud de conocimiento para tomar estas decisiones va más allá de la capacidad cognitiva humana”.
El cofundador de Microsoft aclaró que el cambio no apunta a sustituir a los profesionales, sino a extender su alcance. “Este cambio no es de eficacia, sino de equidad. En lugar de reemplazar al doctor lo multiplicará llevándolo a zonas remotas u hospitales colapsados. La escasez de médicos podría convertirse en un problema del pasado”, agregó.
PUBLICIDAD
En el terreno educativo, Gates imagina tutores digitales capaces no solo de enseñar, sino también de motivar, identificar debilidades y adaptar el aprendizaje en tiempo real. Ya no se trataría de pizarras digitales como símbolo de innovación, sino de una pedagogía algorítmica que podría cuestionar la necesidad misma de la figura del maestro tradicional.
El escenario que proyecta implica un mundo donde los médicos brillantes o los maestros extraordinarios dejarán de ser indispensables, reemplazados por sistemas automatizados que ofrezcan diagnósticos y tutorías hiperpersonalizadas, accesibles para cualquier persona.
PUBLICIDAD
El trabajo filantrópico de Gates en salud infantil
Esta visión sobre la medicina conecta con la labor que Gates lleva adelante a través de su Fundación. Según sus propias afirmaciones, ha ayudado a más de 5 millones de niños de países vulnerables mediante campañas de inmunización y en la lucha contra la malaria, el VIH y la tuberculosis.
Ese trabajo previo explica en parte por qué Gates enfatiza la equidad como el eje central del cambio que viene, más que la eficiencia pura que suele destacarse en otros discursos sobre inteligencia artificial.
PUBLICIDAD
Las advertencias sobre el impacto de la IA en el empleo
No todas las miradas coinciden con el optimismo cauteloso de Gates. Mustafa Suleyman, CEO de IA en Microsoft y autor de The Coming Wave, advierte que esta tecnología no será solo un apoyo para el trabajo humano, sino un reemplazo directo.
Según Suleyman, la inteligencia artificial tendrá un impacto “enormemente desestabilizador” sobre la fuerza laboral, capaz de reconfigurar profesiones enteras y provocar una disrupción inédita en la mayoría de las industrias.
PUBLICIDAD
El propio Suleyman no pone en duda las capacidades de la tecnología, pero sostiene que el rumbo actual conduce a un modelo con menos mano de obra y más control automatizado, lo que a su juicio traerá consigo una inestabilidad sin precedentes.
El verdadero desafío según Gates: el uso de la tecnología
Gates, que dedicó gran parte de su vida a reducir la brecha digital, reconoce que el reto actual ya no pasa por el acceso a la tecnología, sino por el uso que se le da. “A veces, cuando empoderas a los humanos, no siempre se dirige en la dirección correcta”, planteó.
PUBLICIDAD
El dilema, en su opinión, ya no radica en tener herramientas, sino en decidir cómo emplearlas. Como en todas las revoluciones tecnológicas anteriores, el desenlace dependerá de quién tenga el control sobre su desarrollo y aplicación.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Why these 5 books keep readers hooked till the last page
articles.text:
Why these 5 books keep readers hooked till the last page
Discover 5 gripping books readers can finish in one sitting, from unforgettable stories to page-turning plots that make stopping nearly impossible.
There is a special kind of book that makes you forget to check the time. You start reading a few pages, tell yourself you will stop after the next chapter, and suddenly you are halfway through the story. Before you know it, the final page is staring back at you. These are the books that create the rare feeling of being completely absorbed in another world.
In an age of short videos, endless notifications, and shrinking attention spans, finishing an entire book in one sitting might sound difficult. Yet readers continue to crave stories that can hold their attention from beginning to end. The appeal is not necessarily about reading quickly; it is about finding a narrative so compelling that putting the book down feels harder than continuing.
From emotional journeys and unexpected twists to beautifully written stories that demand your attention, these five books have the kind of momentum that can turn “just one chapter” into an entire afternoon or night of reading.
5 Books readers can finish in one sitting
1. The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo by Taylor Jenkins Reid
What if a legendary Hollywood icon finally decided to reveal the truth behind her glamorous life and seven marriages? That irresistible premise lies at the centre of The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo, a novel filled with ambition, love, sacrifice, and carefully guarded secrets.
Its blend of old Hollywood glamour and emotional storytelling creates a compelling narrative that immediately captures attention.
What makes the book especially easy to read in one sitting is the constant sense of mystery surrounding Evelyn’s past. With every chapter, new revelations reshape the reader’s understanding of her relationships and choices. As the pieces of her life story gradually come together, the desire to uncover her biggest secret becomes impossible to resist, making the novel a true page-turner from beginning to end.
2. The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho
Few books demonstrate the power of simplicity quite like The Alchemist. Paulo Coelho follows Santiago, a young shepherd who sets out on a journey after dreaming about a hidden treasure. What begins as a physical search gradually becomes a spiritual journey about purpose, courage, dreams, and listening to one's heart.
The book's short chapters, straightforward storytelling, and philosophical ideas make it incredibly approachable. Yet its simplicity does not make it forgettable. Each stage of Santiago's journey introduces another lesson that naturally pulls the reader forward.
You may begin reading because of the promise of adventure, but you continue because you want to discover what the journey ultimately means. It is the kind of book that can be finished quickly yet leave you thinking about its message long after the final page.
3. Before the Coffee Gets Cold by Toshikazu Kawaguchi
What if you could sit down for one last conversation with someone from your past? Before the Coffee Gets Cold explores this emotional possibility through a small café in Japan where customers can travel back in time under very specific conditions. There is one important rule: no matter what they do in the past, they cannot change the present.
That limitation makes every conversation more meaningful. Instead of focusing on changing history, the characters are allowed to say what they never said or hear what they desperately needed to hear. The novel is divided into interconnected stories, which makes it easy to keep reading from one emotional encounter to the next.
4. The Silent Patient by Alex Michaelides
The Silent Patient has all the ingredients of a book that can turn “one more chapter” into an entire night of reading. The psychological thriller follows Alicia Berenson, a successful painter whose seemingly perfect life changes dramatically when she is accused of murdering her husband.
The most mysterious part is what happens afterwards: Alicia refuses to speak a single word. Her silence becomes the central mystery, leaving readers desperate to understand what really happened.
The story keeps building suspense through unanswered questions, shifting perspectives, and carefully placed revelations. Why did Alicia kill her husband? What happened on the night of the murder? And why has she remained completely silent ever since? As the investigation progresses, every new discovery makes the truth seem even more complicated. With its fast pace, psychological tension, and unexpected twists, the novel creates the kind of momentum that makes putting it down remarkably difficult.
5. The Housemaid by Freida McFadden
If psychological suspense is what keeps you turning pages, The Housemaid delivers exactly that kind of reading experience. Freida McFadden's thriller places readers inside the unsettling world of a housemaid who begins working for a wealthy family and soon realises that the seemingly perfect household is hiding disturbing secrets.
The appeal comes largely from its constant tension and unanswered questions. Just when you think you understand what is happening, another detail changes your perception of the characters or situation. The relatively fast pace makes the story particularly easy to race through, especially for readers who enjoy twists and cliffhangers.
It is the sort of book where stopping at the end of a chapter can feel almost impossible because you need to know what happens next.
Why do some books feel impossible to put down?
The secret is rarely just a complicated plot. Books that readers finish in one sitting usually create a strong combination of curiosity, emotional investment, and momentum. They give you questions you desperately want answered, characters you care about, or situations that make you wonder what could possibly happen next.
In a world filled with distractions, these books offer something increasingly valuable: complete immersion. For a few uninterrupted hours, notifications disappear, time becomes irrelevant, and the only thing that matters is reaching the next page.
And perhaps that is why readers continue to crave books they can finish in one go. It is not simply about finishing a story quickly. It is about finding a story so absorbing that, for a little while, you do not want to do anything else.

articles.title: Llevamos 70 años intuyendo que la vida podría esconderse en las nubes de Venus. Ahora tenemos la primera prueba de laboratorio que lo respalda
articles.text:
Antes de tener conocimientos profundos sobre las circunstancias de cada uno de los planetas del sistema solar, se pensaba que Venus debería ser uno de los mejores candidatos para albergar vida y acoger astronautas viajeros. En principio tenía sentido, ya que es de los que más cerca se encuentran de nosotros. Deberían tener un clima parecido y demás. Hoy en día sabemos que no. Si bien costó estudiarlo por la espesura de su atmósfera, con los años se ha descubierto que es un planeta realmente inhóspito, con temperaturas cercanas a los 500ºC, una presión aplastante y nubes de ácido sulfúrico a su alrededor. Aunque quizás esto último no era tan malo. De hecho, según un estudio publicado recientemente por científicos del MIT, puede que la atmósfera de Venus, incluídas sus nubes corrosivas, sí que podría albergar vida. ¿Significa eso que podríamos vivir en sus nubes? Eso no, pero sí que es un plot twist interesante lo que podría proliferar allí.
Pruebas de laboratorio para imitar la atmósfera de Venus. Estos científicos han imitado en un laboratorio la atmósfera de Venus, replicando nubes con concentraciones de ácido sulfúrico cercanas al 98%. Bajo esas condiciones colocaron una serie de péptidos, que son cadenas pequeñas de aminoácidos. Una versión más pequeña y simple de las proteínas, necesarias para la vida. Quizás hubiese cabido esperar que el ácido sulfúrico, conocido por ser muy corrosivo, destrozase los péptidos. Sin embargo, no solo no los destruyó, como ya se intuía por estudios anteriores, sino que mantuvo su plegamiento.
La paradoja del agua. Curiosamente, los autores de este estudio consideran que es muy posible que esta resistencia de los péptidos al ácido sulfúrico se deba a la concentración casi inexistente de agua que hay en las nubes de Venus. El agua suele ser necesaria para la vida, sí, pero también interviene en las reacciones de hidrólisis que promueven la corrosión del ácido sulfúrico en este tipo de moléculas. Por eso, ante la ausencia de agua, los péptidos se mantienen casi intactos.
El plegamiento importa. En las proteínas, y también en los péptidos, el plegamiento es esencial para que puedan llevar a cabo sus funciones. Por eso, que el plegamiento se mantenga en presencia del ácido sulfúrico es esencial para que la vida pueda proliferar en las nubes de Venus. Y lo cierto es que no sería tan raro que lo hiciese. La atmósfera del planeta vecino tiene unas características de temperatura y presión bastante favorables, especialmente a alturas entre 48 y 60 kilómetros. La superficie sí sería devastadora para la vida, pero en las nubes de ácido sulfúrico quizás podrían proliferar formas de vida que no necesiten el agua.
Quienes ya lo intuyeron. Según explican en un artículo de Universe Today, en 1950, el científico alemán Heinz Haber ya habló sobre la posibilidad de que la vida pudiese abrirse camino en las nubes de Venus. Más tarde, también hablarían sobre el tema tanto Carl Sagan como Harold Morowitz. Aunque es importante dejar claro que no se ha encontrado vida allí y puede que no se encuentre nada nunca, quizás no sea un lugar tan horrible en el que empezar a buscar. Solo había que cambiar el espejo con el que lo miramos.

articles.title: Windows 11 Seems to Be Getting a Battery Widget for the Lock Screen and Widgets Board
articles.text:
Monday, September 7th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Windows 11 Seems to Be Getting a Battery Widget for the Lock Screen and Widgets Board
Microsoft appears to be working on a battery status widget for Windows 11 that would show the charge level of your PC alongside any connected wireless accessories in one place. First spotted on Discord, references to the battery status widget were found in recent preview builds, though the feature isn't functional yet. The widget is designed to appear on both the Widgets Board and the lock screen, with light and dark theme variants already present in the build's assets. It would list the PC's own battery at the top, followed by connected peripherals like Bluetooth mice, keyboards, or headphones, each shown with its own icon, name, and battery percentage. It also looks like it will indicate the charging status and whether Energy Saver is enabled for a given device.
It's a fairly obvious addition and, honestly, quite overdue. Android and iOS have offered similar battery overviews for years, so Windows 11 catching up here isn't exactly groundbreaking. The Widgets Board has struggled to find a real purpose since launching in 2021, with only a handful of apps, such as Phone Link, OneDrive, and Weather, making good use of the space. A genuinely helpful system widget like this one might finally give people a reason to open it. Since none of this is live yet, there's no word on when Microsoft plans to ship it, or whether the lock screen version will roll out at the same time as the Widgets Board one.

articles.title: Pioneer Sphera review: Retrofitting your car with Dolby Atmos
articles.text:
You’ve probably heard spatial audio in your living room or headphones, but what about your car? The Pioneer Sphera is the first aftermarket head unit to integrate Dolby Atmos and true spatial audio, making it a standout in an increasingly narrow field of options for the dashboard.
The Sphera’s actual model name is DMH-WT8000NEX, but Sphera is the branding behind it all, and its namesake is certainly a play on words. Spatial audio is indeed the specialty, which can apply in a virtual sense even without Atmos support, but what makes this system equally interesting is the fidelity it manages to pick up from otherwise pedestrian speakers.
It’s not a cheap upgrade at C$1,800 just for the unit itself — install costs extra unless you do it yourself — but there’s potential here if both Dolby and aftermarket vendors like Pioneer can turn this into something bigger. It does beg the question: Do we even need Dolby Atmos in the car? Your car’s audio setup and your own ears ultimately prove to be the biggest judges.
Going big
The most obvious design point is the 10.1-inch touchscreen, which felt monstrous to me compared to the previous Pioneer head unit I had installed in my 2014 Toyota Corolla LE. That was the AVH-NEX2300 with a 7-inch display. The layout feels somewhat similar, but there’s just so much more going on here.
The first key point to address is which vehicles are most compatible with the Sphera. Pioneer tells MobileSyrup the “sweet spot is roughly 2018 models or older” because they offer the easiest and cleanest installs. There’s the physical install, which in this case is either a standard single/double-DIN covering a wide range of makes and models back then, plus the audio makeup, like accessible front and rear speakers. A crucial underlying element is that the connected phone governs the Dolby Atmos side of the equation, not the car itself. So long as the Sphera fits and there are at least four speakers, you’ve got compatibility.
I didn’t install the unit myself as Pioneer arranged for a professional to do it, but some of the basics do apply, meaning that there’s a microphone snaked along the panels and situated over the rearview mirror. That mic is what picks up voice commands and talking during calls. It can also integrate with a vehicle’s existing Aux-In port, though mine had cable extensions for both Aux-In and USB-A that I could tuck away into the glove box.
Inside the Canadian lab building Dolby Atmos spatial audio into GM vehicles
The Sphera can run both CarPlay and Android Auto to the point where the two almost interchange. Running CarPlay, tap Android Auto on the home screen, tap the Bluetooth icon for the paired Android phone, and it switches over immediately. This is great for those living with others using different platforms, as it means easily switching for any reason. There are other neat combinations that I discovered while using the head unit that I’ll cover further down.
The initial setup isn’t all that detailed, but I do recommend going through the settings, including with an installer, just to make sure you know where everything is. If you’re familiar with Pioneer’s user interface, navigating it probably won’t feel unusual. If you’re not, there are various options to go over.
Setting up Dolby Atmos
This process also doesn’t need much experience to deal with. Plug in the included microphone to the unit and run the Atmos calibration tool onscreen, where it then plays a series of audible tones to measure the cabin space. It’s best to do this last part by getting out of the car so as not to confuse the calibration process with a body or two inside. It takes several minutes to complete, but once done, it’s ready to play anything decoded in Atmos.
Here’s where the caveats start. As of this review, only Apple Music and Audible running through CarPlay can output true Atmos content. Even though both Tidal and Amazon Music offer Atmos-tuned songs on their services, you won’t get the native coding when playing either through CarPlay. Why? Because neither one actually sends over the Atmos-encoded stream to Apple’s car platform. An odd situation given the pieces are there, but that’s where we are right now.
Google already confirmed that Atmos is coming to Android Auto without indicating when it will unlock that feature. The Sphera has its own Stereo Spatial Audio setting that takes in the stereo stream and outputs a spatialized sound out of it. This is wholly virtualized, rather than embedded code, so that’s why the end result doesn’t sound like native Atmos.
Then there’s Bluetooth, and here’s where things get a little interesting. While testing the Sphera, I tried to find ways to get Atmos to play without fully committing to CarPlay. Under default settings on the iPhone, under Music, Dolby Atmos is set to Automatic. However, that only means it’s automatic when connected to compatible AirPods and Beats headphones or earbuds. The Sphera is clearly capable, but the phone doesn’t see it that way because it’s a third-party device. Hence, toggling the setting to Always On forces the compatibility through. Without it, the audio gets downgraded to stereo.
I asked Pioneer about this and here was their response:
“Dolby Atmos is technically possible via Bluetooth, but it is limited to the binaural downmix, specifically for headphones that lack the audio object metadata that is read by the Dolby Atmos engine. Basically, there are spatial cues, but everything is decoded by the iPhone before the stereo audio signal is transmitted over BT. Since SPHERA is not a Spatial Audio enabled BT endpoint, it shouldn’t say Dolby Atmos on the iPhone display, but it still might.”
It certainly did in my case, and sounded like it, too. All the more interesting is that I could listen to Atmos tracks this way while running Waze in Android Auto at the same time. My steering wheel controls could skip or repeat tracks, while phone calls routed through my paired Android phone. This setup opened up another possibility, which was to use an iPad as the audio source. An LTE variant makes this easier, but with a Wi-Fi-only model, I could use my Android phone’s hotspot to bring the iPad online and stream the spatial audio tracks to it.
What Dolby Atmos sounds like in the car
My Corolla is hardly a car stereo stalwart, but the rear speakers at least carry some verve. The thing about Atmos is that it’s only as effective as the speakers allow. You can have spatial audio all day long, but if the speakers suck, then the experience doesn’t feel as enveloping. I will say, though, I liked a lot of what I heard. Yes, the front speakers’ weaknesses become terribly apparent under this scenario, albeit not quite enough to cripple the effect.
I asked Pioneer why the overall sound seemed to be better in a car otherwise untouched from an audio perspective. Sphera delivers a cleaner, lower-distortion signal through a digital signal processor that better balances frequencies to help the speakers sound better. In short, the signal takes some of the load off to enable the speaker to sound a bit better without working as hard.
Additionally, the cabin calibration also acts as a form of audio alignment through Pioneer’s auto-tuning technology, meaning it establishes a baseline equalizer and channel balance to centre the soundstage. That tracks with the cleaner sound I was getting, particularly at higher volumes. Not that I blast music in the car, but my tests did prove I got an upgrade in that department.
The other caveat here is content availability. I’m not a particular fan of how Apple Music lays it out to begin with, but at least there are varieties of spatial audio playlists — all Atmos-ready. My issue is that searching for specific artists or tracks for spatial audio leads to a jumbled mess in the results. Many aren’t Atmos-encoded at all, leaving me scrambling to sort through the playlists and play what I want to hear.
At least it’s worth it when pressing play. I’ve never heard music play quite like this in my aging car. Hearing the way instruments cascade across the speakers is very cool, as is the impressive way Pioneer manages to make vocals feel like they’re coming from the middle, even though there’s no centre channel.
What’s weird about all this is that the makeup feels like it goes against how Atmos is supposed to perform. For years, it’s been about sitting in the “sweet spot” in the centre of the living room. Here, as the driver, I’m sitting on one side towards a corner of the whole setup. That’s what makes the calibration fairly impressive; I didn’t get the sense I was sonically unbalanced.
I’m convinced that vehicles with six speakers or more, and even those with four speakers (or more) and a subwoofer, will feel all this even more than I do. Atmos is clearly built for more than 4-channel arrangements, and that’s where it may provide a whole other audio experience for drivers and passengers.
The benefits of broader compatibility
Who wouldn’t love to use CarPlay or Android Auto on a 10-inch display? The Sphera feels like joining a club for those who routinely do so with factory units in newer makes and models. Split-screen arrangements, particularly in Android Auto, are fabulous given how legible everything is.
I also like that Pioneer’s settings offer plenty of granular control. There’s a 13-band EQ, along with bass and subwoofer controls, to tweak the sound — and doing so doesn’t necessarily mean you have to recalibrate each time. However, I would if you swap out speakers or install a sub, as physical changes to the system usually require a reset that way. You can also play around with Crossover settings by changing listening positions for Atmos tracks to see how it all sounds in different positions inside.
Then there’s the support for hi-res audio. You can do this by plugging in your phone directly or plugging in a USB stick with FLAC and WAV files on it in case you’ve ripped CDs or have a collection waiting to be played. It all sounds great, but again, better speakers will suit this arrangement even better.
Waiting for more players
For now, the Pioneer Sphera is a facilitator seeking compatible partners. Until Android Auto finally gets into the Dolby Atmos game, the head unit’s signature feature is only addressing part of the market. Personally, I don’t see much of a reason to splurge on the Sphera if you don’t intend on listening to Atmos and spatial audio in the car. It truly does set it apart.
On the other hand, if you have a vehicle post-2018, you might not be able to put this in at all. The more complex and computerized vehicles continue to evolve, making it harder it is to swap out the infotainment screen. Like other Pioneer head units before it, the Sphera offers some basic tie-ins to car diagnostics, but it can’t fully replace what comes built-in from the factory.
In that sense, the Sphera is more about stretching out the longevity of an older vehicle than it is about upgrading a newer one. Driving something that’s got some age to it may feel like injecting modern functionality — wireless CarPlay and Android Auto, Atmos, a big display — without buying a new car. Whether that’s worth the asking price comes down to how much you want to change how you listen to audio in the cabin.

articles.title: Microsoft abandonne Office 2021 le mois prochain : cet éditeur prend le relais sur les mises à jour
articles.text:
Cinq ans après sa sortie, Office 2021 arrive au bout du support que Microsoft lui avait promis : le 13 octobre 2026, Word, Excel et consorts recevront leur dernier correctif de sécurité, éditions LTSC comprises. Les logiciels continueront naturellement de fonctionner, mais chaque faille découverte ensuite restera ouverte. C’est là qu’intervient ACROS Security, éditeur slovène connu pour son service 0patch, s’attelant à sécuriser les produits Microsoft que le géant de Redmond abandonné : Windows 7, Office 2016, Windows Server 2012… Office 2021 n’est donc que la continuité d’un travail déjà bien établi, et le passage de flambeau arrive à point nommé.
Ce qui s’arrête le 13 octobre, et ce qui continue
La fin de support ne débranche rien du jour au lendemain : vos applications s’ouvriront le 14 octobre exactement comme la veille (aucun compte à rebours caché dans le code). Ce qui disparaît, c’est le colmatage mensuel des brèches, sur une suite dont les documents piégés, macros et pièces jointes en tête, restent l’un des vecteurs d’attaque préférés des cybercriminels. Microsoft recommande sans surprise de migrer vers Microsoft 365 ou Office 2024, les deux seules branches encore entretenues de la famille.
L’offre de remplacement fonctionne autrement : à partir du 14 octobre, 0patch diffusera pendant au moins trois ans des micropatchs, de minuscules correctifs injectés en mémoire pendant que le logiciel tourne, sans toucher aux fichiers ni exiger de redémarrage. Une rustine posée moteur tournant, en somme. Le périmètre est assumé : uniquement les failles critiques, uniquement sous Windows, sans assistance technique ni nouvelle fonction. Comptez 24,95 € hors taxes par poste et par an avec l’offre Pro, soit un peu moins de 30 € TTC.
Prolonger, racheter, s’abonner : le vrai calcul
Reste à poser les options côte à côte. Conserver Office 2021 sous perfusion 0patch revient à une trentaine d’euros par an, sans rien changer à ses habitudes. Repasser à la caisse pour Office Famille 2024 coûte 149 € en une fois, pour un support qui court jusqu’en octobre 2029, soit un nouveau cycle de trois ans avant de rejouer la même partition. L’abonnement Microsoft 365 Personnel s’affiche à 99 € par an (ou 10 € par mois), stockage en ligne et mises à jour permanentes inclus. LibreOffice, enfin, ne coûte rien et ouvre sans broncher la plupart des documents Office, un candidat sérieux pour l’usage occasionnel.
Les licences dites perpétuelles paient désormais une deuxième fois pour rester sûres, pendant que Microsoft pousse méthodiquement vers l’abonnement, dont les tarifs professionnels français ont d’ailleurs augmenté au 1er juillet (Copilot et Defender en guise de justification). Le prolongement de vie des logiciels abandonnés, lui, devient un marché à part entière. Le précédent Windows 10 a montré qu’un sursis gratuit pouvait exister : sous la pression des associations de consommateurs, les utilisateurs européens y avaient gagné un an de correctifs offerts (et une rallonge jusqu’en octobre 2027). Personne, cette fois, ne semble prêt à monter au créneau pour une suite bureautique.

articles.title: Ya es oficial la nueva powerbank de Ugreen, la primera del mundo con carga inalámbrica en llevar un sistema de refrigeración líquida
articles.text:
Una powerbank es una de esas cosas que te puede venir genial en esos días en los que pasas muchas horas fuera de casa y necesitas batería de sobra. Ugreen tiene un catálogo enorme de estas, pero acaba de estrenar una con 10.000 mAh que cuenta con una novedad muy interesante: utiliza un sistema de refrigeración líquida. Tiene un precio de 129,99 euros, pero usando el código 'DL65062', se queda en 105,99 euros.
UGREEN MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank (10000mAh, Qi2 25W, 45W Built-in USB-C Cable)
Una powerbank con carga inalámbrica y refrigeración líquida
Cuando conectamos una powerbank a un dispositivo, estas se calientan (y por tanto, también hacen que la temperatura del móvil aumente). Esto es malo para la salud de la batería y puede hacer que la velocidad de carga disminuya para proteger la salud de los componentes. Eso es algo que quiere combatir Ugreen con su MagFlow Pro y su sistema de refrigeración líquida.
Este sistema, llamado CryoPulse, tiene una microbomba que hace circular un líquido refrigerante por unos canales térmicos que se pueden ver de forma virtual en el chasis de la powerbank. Esto se suma a una lámina de cobre y un diseño que hace que los componentes tengan una buena separación entre ellos. Es una forma diferente de disipar el calor que la que utilizan normalmente las powerbanks, que es a través de su propio chasis. De esta forma, podemos esperar que no se caliente demasiado incluso en sesiones largas de carga.
Esta MagFlow Pro es compatible con carga inalámbrica Qi2 a 25 W, aunque también tenemos la opción de utilizarla para cargar por cable a 45 W (el cable está integrado). Además, se puede adherir de forma magnética a nuestro móvil, aunque hay que tener en cuenta que su chasis tiene 16,2 milímetros de grosor y pesa 230 gramos.
