articles.title: Nigeria needs 62.5 million NINs in six months to meet target
articles.text:
Nigeria has spent years trying to solve a basic problem of the digital economy: proving who people are. It now has 117.5 million people with National Identification Numbers (NINs), but the latest World Bank assessment suggests the harder part may be turning that scale into a system that is accurate, trusted, and useful.
As of June 30, 2026, the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) had issued NINs to 117.5 million people out of 134.6 million enrolments. The target, backed by the World Bank’s Nigeria Digital Identification for Development (ID4D) project, is 180 million by December 2026.
That leaves Nigeria 62.5 million NINs short, with roughly six months to close the gap. NIMC is currently enrolling between 1.5 and 1.8 million people per month. To reach 180 million by December, the pace would need to rise to about 7.4 million monthly, more than four times the current rate.
NIMC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
The World Bank’s latest implementation report shows substantial progress in building Nigeria’s foundational identity system, but the project remains behind its most ambitious coverage target. At the same time, some of the infrastructure intended to make NIN useful at scale is still being built.
For Kelechi Ndieze, founder and CEO of Africa Tech Factory, the 180 million target is ambitious but necessary given Nigeria’s population and the role a foundational identity system is expected to play.
“Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and its population gives any foundational identity system enormous scale,” Ndieze told TechCabal in an interview on August 31. “I would describe the 180 million target as ambitious, but necessary given Nigeria’s population and the importance of having a functional foundational identity system.”
“A national identity programme cannot be judged only by the number of people captured. We also have to consider whether those identities are unique, accurate, secure and actually usable and verifiable,” Ndieze said.
NIN is moving beyond being a government database to serving as a gateway to financial services, telecommunications, healthcare, social protection, and other digital services. The larger the system becomes, the more costly errors, duplication, weak verification, or security failures can become.
The race for scale
The ID4D project, implemented by NIMC, is a $430 million digital identity programme formally approved in February 2020 and co-financed by the World Bank, the European Investment Bank and Agence Française de Développement. Its objective is not simply to increase the number of Nigerians with NINs, but to establish a robust, inclusive foundational identity system that facilitates access to services.
The project has made significant progress since its October 2019 baseline of 36.9 million NINs. It has licensed 362 front-end enrolment partners, trained nearly 34,000 people, and equipped 46 Nigerian government offices abroad to enrol citizens, according to the World Bank report.
It has also begun connecting NINs to government services. More than 13.4 million people were using digitally enabled services by June, well above the project’s target of three million. NIN-linked services include social cash transfers and health-related programmes. Reaching the remaining population will be harder than building the first 100 million records.
“Ambitious, but not inherently unrealistic,” said Adeoye Abodunrin, an AI and cybersecurity expert, of the 180 million target. “The real question isn’t whether Nigeria can produce 180 million NIN records; it’s whether it can produce 180 million trustworthy digital identities.”
People who remain outside the system are unlikely to be evenly distributed: women, children, people in rural areas, the elderly, undocumented residents and Nigerians in the diaspora can be harder to reach than those already captured.
“The last 20-30 million may be substantially harder than the first 100 million,” Abodunrin said.
That means simply adding more enrolment centres may not be enough. Nigeria will need distributed enrolment capacity, mobile and offline registration, robust biometric processing, and computing capacity to deduplicate records at scale.
The World Bank figures already show gaps in coverage. Women and girls accounted for about 40.4 million of the NINs issued by June, against a target of 79 million. Children under 16 accounted for 26.3 million, against a target of 60.8 million.
NIMC is responding with ward-level enrolment campaigns, additional enrolment partners and plans to procure 7,000 MOSIP-certified devices. It is also offering a 20% premium on enrolment payments for women. The urgency to close the numerical gap creates another risk: that speed begins to take precedence over identity assurance.
Dengiyefa Angalapu, a research analyst at the Centre for Democracy and Development, said Nigeria should be more concerned with the quality of the system than with whether it meets the December deadline.
“I really wouldn’t be worried if the target is not met,” Angalapu said. “I would rather be very, very worried if we don’t have an identity system that is usable.”
The objective, he said, should be to build a system that reliably identifies Nigerians rather than simply reaching a predetermined number.
“It is better that you know 70 Nigerians or even 50,000 Nigerians very well and you can identify them to the core than to have a target of 180 million that you really cannot identify,” he said.
The gap inside the numbers
That concern is also relevant to another figure in the World Bank report: the 17.1 million difference between the 134.6 million people enrolled and the 117.5 million with issued NINs.
The gap does not necessarily mean that millions of people have been excluded. Enrolment captures demographic and biometric information; issuance follows after the record has undergone processing, validation, and deduplication.
“Enrolment is the process of capturing an individual’s demographic and biometric information. Issuance comes after the necessary processing, validation and checks have been completed, while verification happens when issued data can be recognised across multiple systems and sectors,” Ndieze said.
Abodunrin similarly cautioned against treating the gap as an automatic sign of failure. “Enrolment is capturing someone’s data. Issuance happens only after that data clears deduplication against the national database,” he said.
Some friction in the process can signal that controls are working. If every enrolment automatically became a NIN, the system could be more vulnerable to duplicate or poor-quality records.
Angalapu believes the gap could have several causes, from the quality of equipment and training among enrolment agents to deliberate attempts to manipulate the registration process.
NIMC’s decision to expand enrolment beyond its own offices has increased access, but it also places greater responsibility on the quality of the people and equipment used to collect biometric information.
“What’s the quality of the thumbprint that has been taken? What’s the quality of their equipment and all that?” Angalapu said. “All of those can create the gaps that we’ve seen.”
The issue, he said, can also involve deliberate attempts to create false or incomplete identities. The final stretch of the NIN campaign less about simply increasing the number of registration points and more about maintaining consistent identity-proofing standards across them.
For Abodunrin, success should ultimately be measured on five fronts: coverage, uniqueness, accuracy, inclusion and usability.
Building the system behind the number
Nigeria is trying to solve that problem while simultaneously rebuilding the technology underneath its identity system. NIMC’s next-generation National Identity Management System, NIMS 2.0, is being developed around MOSIP, the Modular Open Source Identity Platform. The open-source, modular architecture is intended to provide a more scalable alternative to a system tied closely to proprietary technology.
The World Bank’s August 2026 assessment says the system integrator contract was being finalised, with implementation expected to take about 18 months. That suggests the new architecture is likely to extend beyond the ID4D project’s current December 2026 closing date.
NINAuth, NIMC’s digital identity authentication service, launched in 2025, is also still being refined, with its full integration dependent on the rollout of NIMS 2.0.
The timing creates a difficult situation as Nigeria is trying to dramatically expand the number of identities in the system, while the next-generation infrastructure intended to manage and authenticate them is still under construction.
MOSIP and the sovereignty question
The choice of MOSIP also raises a broader question about digital sovereignty. MOSIP was developed by the International Institute of Information Technology Bangalore (IIIT-B) in India as an open-source alternative to proprietary digital identity systems. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation is a key strategic partner and funder of the project, supporting its development and global expansion.
The platform is designed to give governments greater control over the technology underpinning their national ID programmes and reduce dependence on a single proprietary vendor.
It has been adopted, piloted, or is being explored in 31 countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, including national ID programmes in the Philippines and Ethiopia, and a population registry system in Morocco. Togo, Uganda, Zambia and Nigeria are also at various stages of implementation.
At its core, MOSIP provides software for functions including enrolment, biometric and demographic data management, identity issuance and authentication. However, open source does not automatically mean technological independence.
Abodunrin separates three issues often conflated in discussions about sovereignty: financing, technology provenance and control.
“Taking World Bank money doesn’t mean surrendering control of the data. Using a foreign-built platform doesn’t automatically mean losing control of the infrastructure,” he said.
The real sovereignty test, he said, is technical. “Who holds the data? Where does it sit? Who holds the cryptographic keys? Who has admin access?” he said. “Can Nigeria audit, modify, and run this system if every foreign contractor left tomorrow?”
MOSIP can reduce one traditional sovereignty risk—vendor lock-in—because governments can inspect and adapt an open-source platform. But a country can still become dependent on foreign companies for implementation, maintenance, specialised biometric technology and technical expertise.
“My preferred model is sovereignty by capability rather than sovereignty by geography,” Abodunrin said.
For Nigeria, that would mean retaining domestic control over production data, encryption keys, policy and security operations while building the local expertise required to maintain and eventually extend the system.
Angalapu is less comfortable with the dependence on foreign infrastructure, but sees it as a reflection of Nigeria’s broader technological position.
“As an African, as a Nigerian, I am definitely worried about Nigerian data being hosted somewhere,” he said.
But he also argued that Nigeria cannot simply reject foreign technology without developing viable domestic alternatives.
“This is the Nigerian situation,” he said. “If we say we are worried about that every day, what else can we do?”
He prefers Nigeria to use the current partnership while building the capability to eventually exert greater control over its data and infrastructure. Ndieze takes a similar view, arguing that sovereignty is fundamentally about control rather than where a technology originates.
“Data sovereignty is fundamentally about control, governance and jurisdiction, not simply where the money or technology comes from,” he said.
For him, the important questions are who owns the data, who controls access, where it is stored, who controls the encryption and security infrastructure, who can administer or modify the system and whether Nigeria has the technical capacity to operate it independently.
Nigeria, therefore, does not necessarily need to build every component of the technology itself. But it needs enough technical capability to avoid becoming permanently dependent on the organisations that built or implemented it.
The security problem
That distinction also applies to the security of the identity database. Moving to a new platform may strengthen the underlying architecture, but it cannot, by itself, eliminate the risk of personal data exposure. Identity systems have multiple points of vulnerability: enrolment agents, APIs, authentication services, government institutions, private-sector users, contractors and administrators.
“Technology is only one part of data security,” Ndieze said. “Identity systems are ecosystems.”
Abodunrin makes the same point from a cybersecurity perspective.
“A newer architecture removes legacy vulnerabilities and adds stronger monitoring — real gains,” he said. “But breaches rarely happen inside the core database; they happen across the ecosystem around it.”
That means Nigeria will need more than a modern platform. It will need strong privileged-access controls, encryption, audit trails, API security, continuous vulnerability testing, vendor oversight, insider-threat controls and independent security audits.
Data minimisation is another important safeguard. The less information an identity system collects, the less information is available to steal if one part of the ecosystem is compromised.
NIMC has previously faced allegations and concerns about the handling and exposure of personal information, while maintaining that its core database has not been breached. For citizens, however, the distinction between a breach of the core database and exposure through an API, an agent, or a third party, may matter little.
“They care that their personal information is no longer safe,” Ndieze said.
Angalapu argues that Nigeria should also rethink how it communicates security incidents. A secure database, he said, should not be defined as one that is never attacked. Large identity systems in the United States, Europe and elsewhere have faced attacks and breaches.
The more important question is whether institutions can detect attacks, limit damage and be transparent about what happened.
“It’s actually one that detects these attacks very heavily,” Angalapu said. “But if it happens, you are accountable for how it happened and how you are correcting it.”
The more valuable the identity layer becomes, the more attractive it becomes to attackers. A weakness in a single connected agency or service can expose citizens, even if NIMC’s central infrastructure remains secure.
“The real test isn’t whether NIMC says the new system is secure; it’s whether Nigeria can continuously prove it, through independent assurance and transparent governance, especially when something goes wrong,” Abodunrin said.
From database to digital infrastructure
The ID4D project has already exceeded its target for people using digitally enabled services, while NINs are increasingly being linked to banking, telecommunications, social protection and healthcare systems. Nigeria is therefore moving from building an identity database toward building an identity layer for the digital economy.
The potential benefits are substantial. A reliable foundational ID can reduce duplication, simplify customer verification, improve the targeting of government programmes, and provide financial institutions and public agencies with a common way to establish identity. However, that interconnectedness also raises the cost of failure.
The more services depend on NIN, the greater the consequences of inaccurate records, weak authentication, poor interoperability or a security breach. The race to 180 million should not be judged solely by whether NIMC closes the 62.5 million gap. Nigeria will need to show that the identities being added are unique, accurate, and secure; that they can be authenticated across systems; and that citizens can actually use them.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Huawei, Samsung : ces deux montres connectées valent le détour pendant les French Days 2026
articles.text:
Huawei, Samsung : ces deux montres connectées valent le détour pendant les French Days 2026
Les French Days 2026 cachent quelques bonnes affaires dans l'univers des équipements high-tech, et notamment dans celui des montres connectées. Deux modèles signés Samsung et Huawei se distinguent, pour une rentrée sportive.
L'opération French Days, pour son édition de septembre 2026, passe sensiblement à côté de l'occasion de faire sa rentrée sportive. Les montres connectées en promotion s'y font rares, mais tout de même : en cherchant un peu, on constate que quelques modèles réellement intéressants se cachent dans les listes des revendeurs en ligne. Deux modèles testés par nos soins et qui ont fait leurs preuves à notre poignet se distinguent : la Watch GT Runner 2 de Huawei et la Galaxy Watch 8 de Samsung.
La Watch GT Runner 2, lancée début 2026, nous paraît un bon choix pour les amateurs de course à pied - et l'on sait qu'ils sont nombreux en France - pour peu qu'ils soient plus exigeants sur le terrain du suivi sportif que sur celui de l'écosystème applicatif. Montre Huawei oblige, la tocante se contente d'un portail d'applications limité (dont Spotify ou Deezer sont absents), mais permet de gérer de manière pratique les notifications et de piloter la musique jouée sur le smartphone, indispensable donc lors des sorties sportives. Mais c'est surtout pour la qualité de son suivi cardio et pour la précision de son GPS double-fréquence que ce modèle séduit, sans oublier son autonomie longue durée et son format relativement compact, qui le rend compatible même avec les petits poignets. Si l'appareil a été lancé à 399 €, il s'affiche à 260,19 € dans son coloris noir chez Pixmania. Pour amateurs de couleur, il faudra se tourner vers Amazon, qui propose la version orange de la montre à 291,99 €.
Huawei Watch GT Runner 2
Bien plus généreuse sur le plan applicatif, puisqu'elle tourne sous Wear OS et bénéficie à ce titre de la richesse du Play Store, la Galaxy Watch 8 de Samsung a beau avoir été remplacée par la Galaxy Watch 9 en juillet dernier, elle n'a rien perdu de sa superbe. Dotée d'un bel écran, précise et pourvue d'une large palette de fonctions liées à la santé (scores cardio, possibilité de réaliser des ECG au poignet, index antioxydant...), elle complète avantageusement un smartphone Android. On la trouve, dans le cadre des French Days, à 205,99 € à la Fnac, en version 40 mm et dans son coloris noir. À son lancement, la montre coûtait 299 €.

articles.title: vlt 1.0 Ships as a Drop-in npm Replacement with Phased Installs, Graph Queries, and Malware-Blocking
articles.text:
vlt, the JavaScript package manager and registry built by the original creators of npm, has released vlt 1.0, shipping as a drop-in npm replacement alongside the general availability of its hosted package registries and ecosystem mirrors.
vlt 1.0 introduces several capabilities, including phased installations that stop dependency scripts from running automatically, a queryable dependency graph with more than 60 CSS-like selectors, and hosted registries that reject known-malicious packages before they are served. Founder Darcy Clarke announced the release on X, describing a client "built so nothing runs on your machine just because you typed install."
Where npm downloads, extracts, and runs lifecycle scripts in one step, vlt splits the process in two. vlt install downloads and extracts packages without executing anything, and vlt build then runs scripts only for the packages you trust, skipping anything flagged as malware by default:
$ vlt install # downloads packages, no scripts run
$ vlt build # runs approved scripts, blocks known malware
The second standout is vlt query, a dependency selector syntax that treats the graph like a DOM tree. Around half of the 60-plus selectors are security focused and powered by a Socket integration, letting teams audit dependencies at scale, while a :host(local) selector extends queries across every project on a machine. The --view=mermaid flag renders the matched dependencies as a diagram.
On Hacker News, where the launch reached the front page, one commenter welcomed it as something that "will benefit the entire ecosystem," while others struggled with the pitch, with one asking plainly what the service is and to "pitch me in five seconds or less.", to which Clarke responded:
5s: save time & money
10s: vlt helps engineering teams build JavaScript software faster, reduce supply chain risk, and lower infrastructure costs (via. API perf / payload optimizations).
20s: If you've used npm for years & are just narrowly escaping the various malware attacks or are on the hook for running up CI/agent bills at work because cold installs are X percent of the time compared to your actual builds/runtime, then you should check us out.
After a year of supply chain attacks such as the Shai-Hulud worm, npm v12 now disables install scripts by default, pnpm quarantines fresh releases with a minimum release age, and Bun blocks postinstall scripts too. vlt goes further by rejecting bad packages at the registry, having flagged more than 275,000 package versions, a quarter of which reviewers note are still installable on npm. On raw install speed, though, pnpm and Bun still lead, and vlt reports its registry as up to 38% faster than npm rather than the fastest overall.
For developers who are interested, migrating steps are small and fairly straightforward. After npm install -g vlt, teams can run vlt install and vlt build in an existing project, with configuration moving from .npmrc to vlt.json and a new vlt-lock.json lockfile, as covered in the migration guide. The npm-compatible registry API means existing CI pipelines, private registries, and tooling keep working.
vlt is free and open source under a BSD-2-Clause-Patent license, developed by vlt technology inc. and available now with npm i -g vlt.

articles.title: Robbie Williams-backed Tickets for Good raises €4.5 million for international expansion | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Tickets for Good, a UK startup that provides key workers with low-cost tickets for live events, has raised a further €4.5 million (£3.9 million) to accelerate its international expansion and create 10 new jobs in Sheffield in the next three years.
The funding was secured from NPIF II – Mercia Equity Finance, which is managed by Mercia Ventures as part of the Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund II (NPIF II), alongside Shaping Impact Group (SI3), Finance Yorkshire, Leansquare and private investors.
Steve Rimmer, CEO and co-founder, says: “Tickets for Good was built on a simple belief that live events should be available to everyone, especially the people who give so much to our communities. This investment is a huge vote of confidence in our team, our partners and the impact we’re creating. It will help us grow internationally, create skilled jobs in Sheffield and connect many more people with live events.
“Neville and I started this with a shared love of music and the belief that unused tickets could do something good. Today, that idea has helped more than a million people experience live events they might otherwise have missed, and we’re only just getting started.”
Tickets for Good’s financing sits amid broader investment in technologies supporting events and live fan experiences in Europe.
EU-Startups’ 2026 coverage saw Ghent-based EventTech startup Exhibitly’s €1.4 million pre-Seed round for its AI-powered event personalisation platform, alongside adjacent fan-experience investments such as €6.5 million for Warsaw-based connectivity specialist Microamp, €3.6 million for Lausanne-based immersive-technology startup AlphaLum and €37 million for Amsterdam payments infrastructure company Silverflow.
Together, these financings amount to approximately €50 million.
Chris Borrett, Investment Director at Mercia Ventures, adds: “Demand for live experiences has never been stronger, however rising ticket prices are creating barriers to access for many consumers, while venues and promoters increasingly recognise the value of full attendance and engaged fans. Tickets for Good has created a powerful solution that aligns these interests. We believe the business has the potential to become a category-defining platform within the global live entertainment market.”
Founded in 2022, Tickets for Good distributes surplus tickets donated by event partners to NHS workers, teachers, charity staff and people receiving Cost of Living support. Recipients sign up to the platform for free then pay a nominal transaction fee for each ticket.
It looks to make live events accessible for those who might otherwise miss out, while helping venues maximise capacity, drive ancillary revenues and grow their audiences.
The Sheffield-based company now has almost 750,000 verified members globally and has distributed over 1.25 million tickets.
Robbie Williams is an ambassador for the company, along with former Dutch international goalkeeper Edwin van der Sar and music entrepreneur Hans Brouwer.
Dave Dirks, Managing Partner at Shaping Impact, says: “Tickets for Good is a strong example of the kind of company we want to support: commercially ambitious, highly scalable and built around a clear social purpose. By making live events more accessible to people who too often face barriers to participation, the company is creating meaningful impact in a sector with enormous cultural and social value. We are excited to support the team in this next phase of growth.”
The company expanded into the US in 2023 when it was accepted onto the Comcast SportsTech accelerator in St Louis and now also has operations in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany.
The company also reportedly doubled its revenue in 2025 and aims to achieve a further five-fold growth in the next three years.
Alex McWhirter, CEO of Finance Yorkshire, adds: “In a relatively short space of time, Tickets for Good has achieved significant growth and is now reaching an international audience with its socially driven consumer platform. Finance Yorkshire is pleased to support Tickets for Good in its ambitions to further expand, particularly in overseas markets, and the creation of additional jobs in Yorkshire is particularly welcome.”

articles.title: I tested Kodak’s latest bridge camera with a frankly ridiculous 65x zoom range, and it's ruined my pricey pro lenses forever
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Kodak PixPro AZ653 is one of the best bridge cameras I’ve used and is a great choice for beginners or photographers who want to travel without a bag full of lenses. The massive 65x zoom range is useful when you can’t be sure exactly what subjects you might encounter and want all focal lengths at your fingertips. Image quality is also respectable, despite the tiny sensor, with a usable dynamic range and good resolution. Yes, the pixel count might seem a touch pedestrian in 2026, but Kodak has been wise to resist the allure of headline-grabbing megapixel values and instead focus on building a camera that knows its limitations. The AZ653 isn’t going to replace a mirrorless camera any time soon, but for the price you pay, it does what it sets out to do very well. It’s also a lot of fun and handles beautifully.
Pros
- +Great DSLR-style handling
- +Massive zoom range for safari shots on a budget
- +Sharp optics
- +Effective stabilizer
Cons
- -Tiny 1/2.3in sensor
- -Limited 20-megapixel resolution
- -Zoom is slow to operate
- -Poor LCD quality
Why you can trust TechRadar
Kodak PixPro AZ653: two-Minute Review
If you thought bridge cameras (aka superzoom cameras) were a thing of the past, you’re probably not alone. This area of the photography market hasn’t received too much attention over the past few years, especially now that the lower end of the mirrorless camera arena has some solid options, providing decent specs at a reasonable price.
However, the main selling point of bridges camera has always been the expansive zoom range, something the Kodak PixPro AZ653 has in absolute abundance. The 24-1560mm equivalent zoom lens will cover just about every subject you could possibly hope to encounter, from everyday street scenes to distant wildlife. My favorite lens is my 70-200mm f/2.8 'trinity' zoom, but after having such a long zoom range at my fingertips, it has been tough to go back to a mere 2.8x zoom, even if that lens' wider aperture and quality are streets above for quality.
If you’re after a lightweight camera to take with you on your travels, and you don’t know exactly what photographic opportunities you’re likely to come across, the AZ653 is a petite option that will cover every base.
Autofocus is smooth, if not the fastest you can find on a camera at this price point. It certainly won’t be able to keep up with the fastest animal subjects, so if you’re looking for a wildlife camera, you might be better off with an interchangeable lens model that uses high-end phase detection AF. For slower animals at a distance, however, the massive focal range positions the AZ653 as a good, budget-friendly safari camera.
Image quality, meanwhile, is impressive for a bridge camera, especially one with such a small sensor. The limited area of the chip does place limitations on what the camera can achieve, because of the tiny photo sites, but in good light at least, images are sharp and detailed, even if they do suffer from extreme color noise.
Handling, meanwhile, is decidedly DSLR-like, which is a good thing if you’re used to a larger camera body. It’s comfortable to hold and to operate single-handed, while all of the controls are logically placed. Having a manual control ring on the lens is a huge bonus too, giving the AZ653 a premium edge and a professional look to boot.
It might not be an image quality match for a pro-level mirrorless camera, nor is it going to outgun even the entry-level interchangeable lens offerings from Canon or Nikon, but the Kodak AZ653 is a powerful bridge camera that goes easy on the shoulder and on the bank balance.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Kodak PixPro AZ653: Price and release date
- $449 / £349 / AU$ 750.99
- Available worldwide now
- Limited availability/ backorder lists current in the UK
The AZ653 is designed largely for entry-level users who aren’t ready to invest in an interchangeable lens system, or photographers looking to minimize their kit. The camera is available globally, priced affordably at $449 / £349 / AU$ 750.99.
This makes it significantly cheaper than buying a mirrorless camera with a comparable specification and adding a super telephoto lens. For example, a Canon EOS R100 and RF800mm F11 STM telephoto prime lens would set you back a combined price of approximately $1228 / £1359 / AU$ 2000.
It also costs around 7x less than the Sony RX10 V — a premium bridge camera launched this year, which is superior in most regards except for its lesser zoom range.
- Price score: 4/5
Kodak AZ653: Specs
| Type: | Bridge camera | 
| Sensor: | 20.68MP 1/2.3-inch BSI CMOS | 
| Lens mount: | N/A, Integrated 65x (24-1560mm f/2.9-6.7 equiv) power zoom | 
| Displays: | Main LCD - fixed 3.0-inch LCD (460k dots) | 
| Memory: | SD, SDHC, and SDXC cards up to 1.5 TB (Class 10 or faster recommended) | 
| Video: | Full HD 1080p recording at up to 30 fps | 
| ISO range: | 100-3200 | 
| Burst shooting | 5fps | 
| Processor: | Not specified | 
| Connectivity: | BlueTooth, USB-C, Wi-Fi | 
| Dimensions: | 126.0 x 89.0 x 111.4 mm | 
| Weight: | 20.7oz/588g | 
Kodak PixPro AZ653: design
- Small and lightweight body made possible by the small sensor format
- Reasonable build quality, though mostly plastic
- Fixed 3-inch LCD makes composing shots difficult
Bridge cameras are, by definition, designed to bring together the size and weight benefits of a compact camera with the superior handling characteristics of a DSLR or mirrorless model. By bridging this gap, cameras like the AZ653 are able to offer a generally unrivalled balance of portability and versatility. At least, that’s the objective.
Of course, this was far more of an obvious benefit before the advent of the mirrorless revolution. The difference in size and weight between a Bridge camera and a DSLR such as the Nikon D850 was far more pronounced than between the AZ653 and an entry-level mirrorless model like the Canon EOS R100 or Nikon Z30. Even higher-end cameras like the Canon EOS R6 Mark III, Nikon Z50 II, Sony a7C II, or Fujifilm X-T5 with a standard zoom lens have a comparable footprint.
That last part is important, though. The lens on the AZ653 is anything but standard. As soon as you take the vast zoom range into account, the projected weight differences diverge dramatically. I say projected since the exact dimensions of a mirrorless equivalent to the 65x zoom can only be estimated – no such lens exists.
The EFL (Effective Focal Length) 24-1560mm F2.9-6.7 optic is only possible because of the smaller 1/2.3in sensor at the heart of the camera, and if you were to try and build a similar lens with an image circle big enough to cover an APS-C or full-frame sensor, it would be more like a telescope than a photography optic.
The Kodak AZ653 is well-proportioned and very comfortable to hold. The deep handgrip is reassuring and allowed a firm grip even with my large-ish hands. Despite the body’s small size, there is ample room for around three fingers on the lower part of the grip at one time, while the forefinger sits precisely over the shutter button.
The zoom control surrounds the shutter release and operates with minimal travel, allowing rapid activation of the power zoom. A nice touch is the ability to zoom using the control ring on the lens instead, which is a far more intuitive action for photographers who have committed two-handed camera work to muscle memory. The downside is an artificially long zoom travel; it takes multiple twists of the ring to zoom from the widest focal length to the longest.
The feel of the zoom indicates it's an electronic fly-by-wire system, where the ring isn’t physically connected to anything mechanical, but merely acts as a switch that drives a motor to move the lens elements.
With an optical system this long, the operation is slow and at times, a little stuttery – the zoom stops halfway through its journey and there’s an obvious pause while the onboard computer recalculates where it should be placing the elements. This proved frustrating during my testing, and resulted in multiple missed shots.
Manual focus was a little more successful when using the ring, and I could make relatively precise adjustments. You can access this by moving the position of a switch on the lens barrel, which is another nod to the DSLR influence and adds to the professional experience. The magnified preview image is low-resolution, however, and isn’t especially useful.
The camera features a PASM mode (exposure) dial on the top plate, next to the power button. This provides access to the usual array of control modes, including full Manual and Auto, along with several creative shooting positions, including Scene modes, a Wireless mode for remote operation and file sharing, Movie Mode, Face Beautifier mode for in-camera retouching, and a Custom setting position.
The dial itself is too easily moved in my opinion. In several cases, I’d switched mode without realising, either because I’d nudged the dial with my finger or while getting the camera in and out of my bag, which again meant some missed shots.
The build quality is actually quite good. It is largely made from plastic, but this feels reinforced and not significantly inferior to many recent mid-range mirrorless cameras. I wouldn’t necessarily trust its resistance to rain and dust as such, but the outer shell doesn’t give the impression of cheapness, while the rubberised grip and viewfinder surround lend a more premium edge.
- Design score: 3.5/5
Kodak PixPro AZ653: performance
- The power zoom system is slow, especially when using the lens control ring
- The camera is not as quick to boot up and shut down as comparably priced mirrorless models
- Focus speed itself is quite snappy
With such a long zoom range, there’s always a risk of sluggish autofocus performance. This is often purely because of the additional glass elements needed to provide such a great magnification, making it a more demanding task for the autofocus motors. That being said, the actual dimensions of the optical system are much smaller than the effective image results – the lens is a physical 4.3mm to 279.5mm unit.
As such, the elements are quickly moved into position once the camera has found the correct focus distance, with minimal delay. It’s not quite as smooth as the stepper motors or ultrasonic drives found in many top-level mirrorless optics, nor is it as quiet, but it puts in a respectable performance for the price.
The limiting factor is going to be the autofocus system in the camera itself. Unlike the majority of mirrorless cameras, which use phase-detection AF, the AZ653 shares the slower contrast detection system found in many compact cameras, smartphones and older interchangeable lens bodies.
Without dwelling for too long on the technical specifics, phase-detection autofocus uses specialized sensors to measure the focus position of the lens by looking at how front- or back-focused the light projected through it is. Meanwhile, the AZ653’s contrast-detection AF merely looks for edges of objects in the frame to estimate how far it has to move the lens to get the maximum contrast.
As such, contrast detection has a tendency to hunt, moving the lens elements back and forth to test the correct placement. As expected, this slows down reaction times and isn’t suitable for rapid sports and animal subjects.
The EVF is small but fairly detailed. All of the relevant camera settings are displayed, and it is sharp enough to judge focus with ease. The LCD, on the other hand, is underwhelming. It makes use of only 460K dots, which isn’t enough to accurately assess the quality of captured images.
All files look smudged, not helped by the matte texture of the screen itself. The non-glossy surface makes it easier to preview images in bright light, but critical sharpness is almost impossible to check with any sense of confidence.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Kodak PixPro AZ653: Image quality
- Surprising quality in good lighting
- Mushy JPEGs even at low ISO settings
- Limited to Full HD (1080p) video - no 4K or greater
Image quality is quite surprising. In good light, RAW format files from the AZ653 are rich in detail, and the lens is able to deliver crisp results. Having the RAW capability is a huge bonus and can honestly be considered a staple feature of an enthusiast camera now that many smartphones come equipped with their own RAW mode.
Kodak has been smart not to overstretch the sensor with resolution. The 20 million pixels are more than enough for everyday uses, and by keeping pixel count lower than most APS-C and Micro 4/3 cameras, the AZ653 is able to maintain a workable level of noise control and a reasonable dynamic range.
Sure, highlights clip more easily than when shooting the same scene on both the AZ653 and an APS-C model like the 26MP Fujifilm X100VI, but the performance is better than many larger-sensor cameras of last decade.
In-camera JPEG shooting is a different matter, and the quality is far less impressive. Default noise reduction is too aggressive and fine detail is rapidly obliterated, creating a smudged look common to compact cameras. Color noise reduction itself isn’t especially effective either, leaving behind too many colored blotches.
When shooting RAW, I was able to increase the ISO to about 800 before grain became a major problem which is, once again, impressive. My advice would be to increase the sensitivity of the AZ653 rather than to brighten underexposed RAW files — unlike many of the more ISO-invariant cameras we see today — this should produce a better balance of image texture and noise pattern.
Regarding lens quality, sharpness does drop off towards the long end of the zoom range. The slightly blurred results reminded me of shots taken with a budget Tamron 70-300mm DSLR lens I used to own back in the day – fine detail just isn’t present, almost as if your shots were taken through a greasy window. Files are usable on Instagram, but won’t be suitable for prints.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
- Image quality score: 3/5
Testing Scorecard
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
| Price | Many smartphones will give you better quality, but not a 1560mm lens for less than $500. | 4/5 | 
| Design | I love the deep handgrip and tactile control ring – both premium flourishes. The poor LCD is disappointing though. | 3.5/5 | 
| Performance | The processing power is limited and startup/ shutdown and operation is slow | 3.5/5 | 
| Image quality | It's passible in good even light, but the small photosites can't keep up after dark | 3/5 | 
Should I buy the Kodak PixPro AZ653?
Buy it if…
You need a huge zoom range without the cost
Let's be honest, you aren't going to find this kind of magnifying power for a DSLR or mirrorless camera for less than five to ten times the price. If you're heading off on safari, this might be the best option for your budget.
You need a portable camera with decent handling
The deep handgrip and button positions give the AZ653 a distinctly DSLR-like feel, and it's all the better for it. If you like the convenience of a compact but the handling of a bigger camera, this will serve you right.
You mainly shoot for social media
If you mostly just upload your images to Instagram or shoot reels for TikTok, the quality you can get from the AZ653 will be more than adequate
Don’t buy it if…
You shoot a lot of portraits
The small sensor provides great magnification, but the downside is heavily reduced depth-of-field control. Even at the max aperture backgrounds are hard to blur, making environmental portraits unappealing.
You need absolute image quality
There are smartphones with much bigger sensors out there, such as the iPhone 17 Pro, and you might have that with you for everyday tasks anyway. The AZ653 struggles above ISO800 and out-of-camera JPEGs are sometimes terrible 
You want to expand a camera system
The Kodak AZ653 is a great first camera, but you can pick up an entry-level mirrorless camera for similar money, especially second-hand. Yes, you'll lose the 65x zoom, but if you don't routinely shoot cheetahs from afar, you won't miss this. A mirrorless system will allow you build a lens collection from the start.
Also consider
Nikon Coolpix P1100
It's a bit pricier, at around $900 - $1000, but this buys you an even greater 125 x zoom up to 3000mm EFL, an f/2.8 maximum aperture, 4K UHD video, and a 3in articulating, 921k-dot LCD screen. You still have to make do with a 1/2.3in sensor though, and an even lower 16 megapixel resolution.
Read our Nikon P1000 review
Sony RX10 V
Considered the best bridge camera ever made, this is a serious piece of kit. Featuring a 1-inch stacked sensor and a 24-600mm lens, it still gives you a good focal range, while also offering bigger pixels for better light-gathering and signal-to-noise ratio. It's anything but cheap though; expect to pay about the same as for an entry-level full-frame mirrorless camera.
Read our Sony RX10 V review
How I tested the Kodak PixPro AZ653
- I spent around two and a half weeks with the AZ653
- Images were taken in both good light and low-light conditions, shooting in JPEG mode and RAW
- Most images were shot handheld to test the usability at longer focal lengths
I spent several weeks shooting with the PixPro AZ653, taking in multiple different lighting conditions. I shot in both JPEG and RAW formats to see how differently the built-in processing algorithms might process the images to my own RAW workflow.
Since one of the reasons to buy a bridge camera is for weight saving, I decided to shoot mainly handheld, as this would be how many users would experience the camera. I wanted to thoroughly check the ease with which someone might capture sharp images at the longer focal lengths.
I mainly used Aperture Priority (A) and Manual (M) modes for both creative freedom and to test the auto exposure systems.
To explore the noise performance, I shot with the camera at each ISO setting, from 100 through to 3200, using a tripod to ensure any drop in sharpness was not due to camera shake at the lower sensitivities. I also worked through the focal range, capturing the same scenes from the widest to the longest zoom settings.
First reviewed: September 2026
Peter is a photographer, writer, and journalist who served as Editor for Digital Photographer Magazine, working on the title for 8 years.

articles.title: Montech Century II Gold 850W power supply review: Excellent budget-friendly Gold-tier ATX 3.1 unit with Cybenetics Platinum efficiency
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Montech Century II Gold 850W ATX 3.1 lands squarely in the sweet spot of the mainstream Gold tier. Its half-bridge LLC platform from XWY is not the most ambitious silicon configuration you can buy, but the unit delivers solid voltage regulation, respectable ripple suppression, and Cybenetics ETA Platinum efficiency at both 115V and 230V input. At its $90 current retail price, it punches well above its weight against significantly pricier competition while bundling a native 12V-2x6 cable, a Zero-RPM Fan mode, and a ten-year warranty.
Pros
- +Excellent $90 value
- +Native 600W 12V-2x6 connector
- +Cybenetics Platinum certified
- +100% Japanese capacitors
- +Quiet Smart Zero RPM Fan
- +Fully modular
- +Vast OCP/OPP headroom
- +10-year warranty
Cons
- -Second-tier secondary capacitors
- -Slightly longer than standard
- -Mediocre-quality silicon
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Montech is one of those brands that, despite a relatively recent international profile, traces its lineage back through the Taiwanese components industry to engineers with three-plus decades of experience. The company formally took shape in 2016 and entered Western retail channels around 2019, initially building its name on aggressively priced PC cases. From that beachhead, Montech expanded methodically into air and liquid coolers, fans, mechanical input devices, and, most relevant for this review, power supplies.
The original Century line positioned Montech at the value-conscious end of the PSU market. At the same time, the more recent Titan series advanced to premium territory by relying on Seasonic and CWT for its underlying platforms. The Century II line, refreshed for ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 with native 12V-2x6 connectivity, sits between those bookends. It is meant to deliver modern-spec compliance and Gold-level efficiency at a price point that undercuts the established premium players by a meaningful margin. The 850W model is the entry point of the family, and today we examine whether it belongs among our list of best power supplies on the market.
Specifications and Design
| Montech Century II Gold 850W ATX 3.1 Power specifications (Rated @ 40 °C) |  |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAIL | +3.3V | +5V | +12V | +5Vsb | -12V | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MAX OUTPUT | 20A | 20A | 70.8A | 3A | 0.3A | 
| Row 1 - Cell 0 | 100W | 100W | 849.6W | 15W | 3.6W | 
| TOTAL | 850W | Row 2 - Cell 2 | Row 2 - Cell 3 | Row 2 - Cell 4 | Row 2 - Cell 5 | 
| AC INPUT | 100 - 240 VAC, 50 - 60 Hz | Row 3 - Cell 2 | Row 3 - Cell 3 | Row 3 - Cell 4 | Row 3 - Cell 5 | 
| MSRP | $90 | Row 4 - Cell 2 | Row 4 - Cell 3 | Row 4 - Cell 4 | Row 4 - Cell 5 | 
In the Box
The Century II 850W ships in a tidy cardboard box dressed in a charcoal/silver color scheme that attempts to mirror the unit's own finish. Montech leans hard on the dual certification story up front, with the 80Plus Gold and Cybenetics Platinum badges both printed prominently on the box face, alongside the ten-year warranty claim and references to the ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 standards. Foam inserts protect the PSU itself.
Bundled accessories are beyond modest, especially for the price range of the unit. We found the AC power cable, a sleeve of mounting screws, a few reusable Velcro-style cable straps, a few cable ties, and a small user manual. At this price point, that is an unexpectedly good unboxing experience.
The cable bundle itself is all-black and entirely flat-ribbon in construction. The native 12V-2x6 cable is the highlight, rated at the full 600W of the connector standard. Buyers get two 6+2-pin PCIe cables carrying four connectors total, two EPS 8-pin runs for CPU power, two SATA chains with four connectors apiece, and a single Molex chain. The total connector count covers every realistic single-GPU configuration this PSU should be paired with, including current-generation cards with multiple PCIe inputs.
| Montech Century II Gold 850W ATX 3.1 |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Connector type | Hardwired | Modular | 
| ATX 24 Pin | - | 1 | 
| EPS 4+4 Pin | - | - | 
| EPS 8 Pin | - | 2 | 
| PCI-E 5.1 (12V-2x6) | - | 1 | 
| PCI-E 6+2 Pin | - | 4 | 
| SATA | - | 8 | 
| Molex | - | 4 | 
| Floppy | - | - | 
External Appearance
At 160mm in length, the Century II 850W is a touch longer than the ATX guideline 140mm reference, though well within what any modern mid-tower will accept without complaint. Compact-case builders should double-check clearances before committing.
Visually, this is one of the most distinctive units in its class. Where the vast majority of competitors stick to plain black sheet metal, Montech has gone with a two-tone treatment: a matte silver top panel cut with a geometric triangular grille that looks like an architectural detail more than a fan vent, paired with a black chassis body. Both side panels carry a subtle, debossed angular pattern and the Century II wordmark, while a discrete "Montech" logo is along the bottom edge. The finish is clean, and the panel gaps are tight.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The rear face holds the AC receptacle and the primary on/off switch, plus a smaller secondary toggle that lets the user disable the hybrid mode and run the fan continuously if they prefer. That second switch is something Montech could easily have buried, and it is a small feature but one we are glad to see. At the front, we can only see the modular connectors with their silkscreened labels that clearly identify each socket. Connector keying makes mis-insertion practically impossible anyhow.
Internal Design
Cooling falls to a 135mm Hong Hua HA13525M12SF-Z fan, which uses a fluid-dynamic bearing engine. The model designation indicates a medium-speed variant rather than the higher-rated H-series spindle some premium Hong Hua models employ, but the maximum speed of 2000 RPM is very high. In practice, fluid-dynamic bearings are the right choice for a unit pitched for long service life, and the fan curve of this unit is calibrated conservatively enough.
The OEM is Shenzhen Xinweiye Technology Co., typically referred to as XWY. XWY is not as familiar a name as Seasonic, CWT, or Great Wall, but the company has been quietly supplying Montech's Century II family and a handful of other brands' mainstream ATX 3.x designs.
Filtering on the AC inlet PCB consists of four Y capacitors, two X capacitors, and two filtering inductors – a good, complete configuration for a unit at this wattage. The two bridge rectifiers sit on the large heatsink across the unit’s edge, sharing it with the APFC stage components. The APFC stage uses a typical inductor paired with two bulk capacitors mounted side by side, one from Rubycon and one from Nippon Chemi-Con, both branded for 105°C operation. These are two of the most reputable Japanese manufacturers, in line with Montech's marketing claim of 100% Japanese capacitors, although the products themselves are extremely unlikely to have been made in Japan nowadays.
The primary inversion stage topology is a half-bridge LLC with two PIP Semiconductor SPTA65R130FDD MOSFETs, entirely appropriate for the price point and well-proven at this output rating. The main transformer sits centrally on the board with gold tape insulation, dividing primary from secondary. The rectification stage on the secondary side is handled by six SPTJ04R014E MOSFETs operating in synchronous-rectifier mode. 3.3V and 5V is generated through typical DC-to-DC conversion, but unlike the commonly found vertical daughterboard, all components are on the main PCB.
Secondary-side electrolytics are predominantly TK-branded, which corresponds to the Japanese manufacturer Toshin Kogyo. TK is genuinely Japanese, which validates Montech's marketing copy, but enthusiasts should be aware that Toshin Kogyo is widely regarded as a second-tier domestic capacitor brand rather than a peer of Nippon Chemi-Con, Rubycon, or Nichicon. Then again, TK’s reputation is solidly higher than that of the manufacturers supplying the silicon of this unit. In practical terms, the unit should age perfectly well, but it is a tier below what the higher-end competition uses (and that is reflected in the price).
Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)
Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)
For the testing of PSUs, we are using high-precision electronic loads with a maximum power draw of 2700 Watts, a Rigol DS5042M 40 MHz oscilloscope, an Extech 380803 power analyzer, two high-precision UNI-T UT-325 digital thermometers, an Extech HD600 SPL meter, a self-designed hotbox, and various other bits and parts.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
At 115 VAC, the Century II 850W averaged 90.5% efficiency across the 10-100% load range during cold testing. At 230 VAC, the figure rose to 92.5%. Both numbers comfortably exceed the Cybenetics Gold threshold, with Cybenetics independently certifying the unit as Platinum across both input voltages. The unit holds 80Plus Gold certification under the 115V input voltage because it does not meet the 100% load efficiency requirement for the 80Plus Platinum badge, which is why Montech labels it Gold rather than Platinum on that scheme. The Cybenetics methodology, which considers the average efficiency rather than the four-point 80Plus protocol, reflects the platform's strengths more accurately. The efficiency curve peaks just below the 50% load mark and stays largely flat from there through the upper end of the range.
Fan behavior under cold conditions is adequately good. The smart fan mode keeps the rotor stationary at the lowest load points, and even after the fan begins spinning, the noise floor stays well under the threshold of audibility in a typical desktop environment. There is a ramp toward maximum output, but the fan does not approach anything resembling a high RPM during room-temperature testing. Internal temperatures climb predictably with load but remain well within the comfort zone of the components throughout.
Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)
Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)
Inside the hot box, the average efficiency at 115 VAC fell to 89.2%, while 230 VAC operation averaged 91.1%. The roughly 1.3-1.4 percentage-point degradation is not small but is in the expected range for a Gold-tier 850W design under sustained elevated ambient conditions. The unit shrugged off the thermal stress impressively, better than we thought it would after checking its parts.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The fan ramp under hot conditions is, as expected, much steeper than under cold testing. The fanless operation threshold moves down, and the speed curve becomes more aggressive. The fan reached its maximum rated speed at maximum load. The heatsink temperatures we measured are fair, suggesting that the platform has a cooling margin but largely depends on its massive fan for cooling.
PSU Quality and Bottom Line
Power Supply Quality
Electrical performance is solid across the board. Voltage regulation sat at 0.4% on the 12V rail, 0.5% on the 5V rail, and 0.4% on the 3.3V rail across the 20-100% load range. Those numbers are well below the ATX specification recommendations and demonstrate that the unit is extremely well-tuned. They do not match the absolute best units we have tested, but they are firmly in exceptional territory for a Gold-class design.
Ripple suppression follows a similar pattern. At 100% load, the 12V rail peaked at 30 mV, the 5V at 24 mV, and the 3.3V at 22 mV. All of these figures sit well inside ATX limits (120 mV on 12V, 50 mV on the minor rails). They are not the cleanest numbers we have ever seen, but they are clean enough that system components will see a stable, quality power supply.
During our thorough assessment, we evaluate the essential protection features of every power supply unit we review, including Over Current Protection (OCP), Over Voltage Protection (OVP), Over Power Protection (OPP), and Short Circuit Protection (SCP).
All four protection mechanisms triggered correctly during our hot-box stress runs. OCP on the 3.3V and 5V rails sat at 154% and 150%, respectively, with the 12V triggering around 126% of its nominal rating. OPP triggered at approximately 124% of the 850W output during hot testing, which translates to roughly 1,050W of sustained delivery before the unit pulled the plug. That is a substantial cushion. The minor rails in particular carry far more headroom than the nameplate implies, and even the 12V rail tolerates well over its rated current before tripping.

Bottom Line
At its $90 pricing at the time of this review, the Century II 850W is one of the most aggressively priced ATX 3.1 units with a native 12V-2x6 connector and Cybenetics Platinum-equivalent efficiency on the market. Competition at that price point exists but is genuinely thin once you start filtering for fully modular, all-Japanese capacitor designs with a decade of warranty coverage. Especially at the $80 sale price that it reaches periodically, it becomes a borderline default recommendation for mid-range 5070-tier and 9070-tier builds.
The performance picture is a study in restraint. Voltage regulation and ripple suppression are not class-leading, but they surely are exceptional. Efficiency comfortably exceeds the Gold thresholds across almost all of the load range, easily granting the platform a Platinum certification badge when the average efficiency is the primary factor. Fan management is quiet, and the Smart Zero mode behaves the way the marketing claims.
Where the unit shows its budget positioning most clearly is in the platform and silicon. XWY is a less established OEM than Seasonic or CWT, much of the silicon comes from relatively unknown Chinese manufacturers, and TK secondary capacitors - while genuinely Japanese - are not Nippon Chemi-Con. None of these are problems per se but simply the cost-engineering decisions that make the $90 price possible. The 10-year warranty is the strongest signal that Montech itself expects the platform to age gracefully, and that warranty length is a meaningful feature, not marketing decoration.
Taken on its own terms, the Century II 850W ATX 3.1 unit is exactly the unit Montech intended to build: a no-nonsense, modern-spec, Gold-tier 850W power supply that does not try to compete with the premium tier on engineering pedigree, but does compete, and very effectively so, on overall value. It is the sort of PSU we expect to see in a lot of mainstream builds over the next few years, and there are worse fates than that for any product.

articles.title: Cientista-chefe da OpenAI pede cautela com avanço da IA
articles.text:
O cientista-chefe da OpenAI, Jakub Pachocki, publicou no domingo (6) um ensaio em que alerta para o ritmo de evolução da inteligência artificial (IA) e defende maior cautela no desenvolvimento de sistemas cada vez mais capazes. No texto, publicado no site da própria OpenAI, o pesquisador afirma que o avanço pode chegar ao ponto de permitir que as máquinas participem cada vez mais do próprio processo de desenvolvimento.
Pachocki afirma que, com base em resultados internos, tem forte expectativa de que o ritmo atual de progresso possa continuar até o chamado autoaperfeiçoamento recursivo (recursive self-improvement, ou RSI). Nesse cenário, sistemas de IA passariam a impulsionar cada vez mais o próprio desenvolvimento. Para o cientista, esse caminho exige intervenções mais amplas para garantir que o avanço da tecnologia permaneça sob controle humano.
IA está mais difícil de compreender
No ensaio, Pachocki descreve uma mudança ocorrida desde 2023, quando resultados do projeto de pesquisa RLSlow deram à equipe confiança de que seria possível ampliar o treinamento de modelos de raciocínio. Três anos depois, segundo ele, esses sistemas já conseguem operar computadores e interfaces gráficas, colaborar com pessoas e outras IAs e realizar projetos de pesquisa.
O cientista também aponta avanços nas capacidades relacionadas à segurança cibernética. Ao mesmo tempo em que os modelos se tornam mais capazes, Pachocki afirma que seus resultados ficam mais difíceis de interpretar. Para ele, a inteligência produzida pelo deep learning não é diretamente comparável à humana e, conforme a IA supera pessoas em mais áreas, fica mais difícil determinar exatamente do que os sistemas são capazes.
Essa dificuldade está relacionada ao próprio funcionamento dos modelos. Pachocki afirma que a IA é mais “cultivada” do que projetada, sendo resultado da repetição de processos de otimização em grandes quantidades de computação. Segundo ele, os sistemas são extremamente complexos e seu funcionamento geral ainda não pode ser completamente descrito ou compreendido.
Alinhamento ainda é um desafio
Outro ponto central do ensaio é o alinhamento da IA, conceito usado para descrever o esforço de fazer com que os sistemas ajam de acordo com padrões e objetivos considerados adequados pelos humanos. Pachocki diferencia o alinhamento de objetivos, relacionado a executar aquilo que foi determinado, do alinhamento de valores, ligado à capacidade de generalizar princípios para situações novas ou ambíguas.
O problema, segundo ele, é que sistemas mais inteligentes passam a atuar em ambientes diferentes daqueles encontrados durante o treinamento. Isso pode dificultar a generalização dos valores ensinados aos modelos. Pachocki afirma que futuras IAs precisam manter valores humanos mesmo quando não acreditarem estar sob supervisão humana.
A OpenAI utiliza diferentes abordagens para tentar lidar com essa questão. Uma delas é o monitoramento do chamado chain of thought, ou cadeia de pensamento, que permite analisar o processo de raciocínio verbalizado dos modelos. Pachocki, porém, afirma que as avaliações da empresa indicam que a capacidade de depender desse monitoramento está diminuindo progressivamente.
Entre os motivos estão o uso dos modelos em ambientes mais complexos, a capacidade crescente das IAs de raciocinar sobre o próprio processo de raciocínio e o aumento da inteligência dos sistemas mesmo sem o uso de raciocínio verbalizado.
Por que continuar desenvolvendo modelos mais poderosos?
Apesar dos alertas, Pachocki não defende simplesmente interromper o desenvolvimento. Ele considera que há um argumento forte para continuar treinando modelos mais inteligentes rapidamente: criar sistemas de defesa contra os riscos provocados por outras IAs.
O cientista destaca especialmente a cibersegurança. Segundo ele, os modelos estão se tornando sobre-humanos na capacidade de invadir e sair de sistemas computacionais, ampliando o alcance dos riscos associados à tecnologia. A OpenAI, afirma Pachocki, precisa usar os modelos mais avançados disponíveis para reforçar a segurança de infraestruturas críticas.
Ao mesmo tempo, ele afirma que a necessidade de construir defesas não pode servir como justificativa para um avanço imprudente. Para Pachocki, a ideia de avançar “a qualquer custo” deixa de fazer sentido diante da dimensão dos riscos envolvidos.
OpenAI discute desaceleração do desenvolvimento
É nesse contexto que Pachocki aborda diretamente o autoaperfeiçoamento recursivo. Ele afirma que, caso o progresso da IA continue, a participação das máquinas no próprio desenvolvimento tende a aumentar e o RSI poderá ocupar um papel central nas futuras descobertas científicas.
O pesquisador diz que a comunidade pode escolher entre duas alternativas principais: conduzir o processo de forma a fortalecer simultaneamente alinhamento e monitoramento, mantendo pessoas envolvidas no ciclo de desenvolvimento, ou coordenar uma desaceleração do avanço enquanto se busca maior confiança nas medidas de segurança. Para Pachocki, a melhor opção atualmente é combinar as duas abordagens.
Ele também defende que o avanço dos sistemas seja condicionado à confiança existente nas medidas de segurança. Segundo Pachocki, compromissos como o Preparedness Framework, da OpenAI, e o Responsible Scaling Policy, da Anthropic, deveriam evoluir para parâmetros de segurança amplamente adotados para permitir a continuidade do desenvolvimento. Esses critérios poderiam ser fiscalizados por auditorias independentes, governos ou organismos internacionais.
No fim do ensaio, Pachocki afirma que nenhum laboratório resolveu alinhamento e monitoramento em grau suficiente para continuar aumentando a escala da IA na velocidade máxima por muito mais tempo. Ele diz esperar que desacelerações voluntárias se tornem comuns até que existam parâmetros de segurança compartilhados e defende que a coordenação internacional sobre o desenvolvimento futuro da IA se torne uma prioridade para governos.
O cientista também afirma que o objetivo da automação da pesquisa em IA não deve ser apenas alcançar sistemas mais inteligentes, mas fazer isso de uma maneira que mantenha as pessoas envolvidas no processo de melhoria contínua e preserve o controle humano sobre o futuro.
Ana Figueiredo é repórter de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Si quieres un buen iPhone, no merece la pena esperar: el iPhone 17 Pro está más barato que nunca en Amazon
articles.text:
Sí, estamos a solo dos días de que salga el iPhone 18 Pro, pero si lo que tú quieres es un buen iPhone, te gusta el diseño de la última generación y prefieres ahorrar algo de dinero, Apple acaba de ponerte sobre la mesa una de las mejores ofertas del año. El iPhone 17 Pro está al precio más bajo de la historia en Amazon. Y, si bien es un escenario que se suele dar cuando el nuevo modelo está a la vuelta de la esquina, este año tiene aún más sentido sacrificar esas mejoras que se esperan e ir a por un dispositivo un poco más barato.
¿Por qué? Bueno, es bien sabido que el diseño del iPhone 17 Pro se mantendrá en el nuevo modelo. En este sentido, las únicas novedades vendrán por el lado del color: se espera que Apple lance el iPhone 18 Pro en burdeos, azul cielo y un tercero que podría ser el clásico plateado o el negro.
Sí estarán presentes otro tipo de novedades, pero no se espera que estas sean tan avanzadas como para diferenciar tanto ambas generaciones. En otras palabras: puedes ahorrar algo de dinero si optas por el iPhone 17 Pro sin tener esa sensación de haber tenido algo mucho mejor por un poco más.
iPhone 17 Pro de 256 GB - Completamente nuevo y con garantía de 3 años.
*Los precios pueden haber cambiado desde la publicación
Este año tiene aún más sentido. Puede que 140 euros de ahorro no parezcan demasiado, y otros años la recomendación puede haber sido diferente, pero con el iPhone 18 Pro la cosa cambia. Está casi confirmado que Apple subirá el precio de los dos móviles, por lo que si quieres lo último de lo último, tendrás que pagar la diferencia de la oferta y, además, el aumento que considere la compañía.
Todas las filtraciones auguran que el iPhone 18 Pro subirá entre 150 y 250 euros, por lo que el ahorro podría ser significativo por renunciar a un par de mejoras en la cámara, un chip un poco más potente y la opción de elegir los nuevos colores.
En estos momentos puedes comprar el iPhone 17 Pro en Amazon por 1.179 euros en los tres colores disponibles y con 256 GB de almacenamiento. ¿Es la oferta del año? 140 euros de ahorro no es la panacea, pero nunca antes había estado tan barato en Amazon.
¿Merece la pena esperar al nuevo iPhone?
Por supuesto, todo depende del tipo de usuario que seas. Tener el último modelo siempre es una ventaja para probar las últimas novedades, pero sabiendo que Apple lanzará una generación bastante continuista, optar por el iPhone 17 Pro es una muy buena opción.
Seguirá siendo totalmente compatible con iOS 27, Siri AI, todas las opciones de Apple Intelligence, se actualizará durante años y su cámara debería tener poco que envidiar a la del iPhone 18 Pro. En cambio, esos 300-350 euros de ahorro y el hecho de poder tenerlo mañana mismo en la mano pueden ser más que suficientes para dar el paso, renunciar a las novedades y tener un iPhone que sigue siendo uno de los mejores móviles del momento.
Si no crees que puedas sacarle todo el partido a la cámara del móvil y los nuevos colores no te convencen demasiado, nuestra recomendación, si necesitas un iPhone ahora mismo, es que optes por el iPhone 17 Pro: te ahorrarás dinero, lo tendrás mañana en tu casa y difícilmente sentirás que estás haciendo una mala compra incluso cuando Apple anuncie el nuevo modelo en un par de días.

articles.title: J'ai essayé une console Acer qui cache un vrai PC sous l'écran : et si c'était la solution qu'on attendait ?
articles.text:
Acer a fait de l’IFA son terrain de jeu favori pour dévoiler des concepts hors normes. Cette année, le constructeur taïwanais s’attaque au bouillonnant marché des consoles portables avec le Project DualPlay Mini. Une machine étonnante qui promet de fusionner l’expérience gaming nomade avec la productivité d’un véritable ordinateur. Nous avons pu manipuler ce prototype très prometteur.
Un gabarit massif, mais une prise en main préservée
Le Project DualPlay Mini impose sa présence dès le premier contact via son écran de 8 pouces, mais surtout en raison de ses mensurations et de son épaisseur bien supérieures aux standards actuels que sont le Steam Deck ou la ROG Ally. Dans les faits, on se rapproche davantage de l’encombrement d’une Lenovo Legion Go.
Pourtant, cette épaisseur notable n’handicape pas vraiment l’ergonomie générale. Les joysticks asymétriques tombent bien sous les pouces, les gâchettes sont réactives, et quelques minutes d’utilisation suffisent à rassurer : la console tient bien en main.
Le tour de magie : un PC sous l’écran
Si le châssis est si épais, c’est pour abriter la véritable innovation de ce concept. Le Project DualPlay Mini cherche à résoudre le plus gros défaut des consoles sous Windows 11 : l’absence de clavier physique, ce qui rend la navigation souvent infernale.
Ici, l’écran pivote sur lui-même et coulisse vers le haut pour révéler un véritable clavier rétroéclairé intégré au châssis. La bascule entre la session de jeu et le mode bureautique se fait en une seconde. Malgré le format compact, la frappe s’avère correcte et la course des touches suffisamment rapide pour taper un mail, naviguer sur le web ou gérer ses fichiers avec un confort inespéré sur ce type de machine.
Une fiche technique musclée sous le capot
Si Acer est resté publiquement très discret sur les entrailles de sa machine, parlant simplement d’un partenariat avec Intel, nous avons pu vérifier les caractéristiques techniques qui animent ce prototype. Et le constructeur n’a pas fait les choses à moitié.
Le Project DualPlay Mini est propulsé par un processeur Intel Arc G3, couplé à un GPU Intel Arc B370 (128 MB). Pour soutenir le tout, on retrouve pas moins de 32 Go de RAM moulinant à 8533 MT/s. Une configuration particulièrement véloce, refroidie par un système à double ventilateur (dont un AeroBlade métallique), indispensable pour faire tourner la double casquette gaming et productivité de l’appareil.
Un concept hybride qui laisse rêveur
Bien qu’il s’agisse d’un prototype sans date de sortie ni prix annoncés, le Project DualPlay Mini est l’une des propositions les plus intéressantes de ce salon. En effaçant la frontière entre la console de jeu et l’outil de travail nomade, Acer apporte une vraie solution pertinente, et ergonomique, à un problème connu. Reste désormais à voir si le constructeur parviendra à affiner le design de sa machine pour la rendre un peu plus passe-partout avant une éventuelle commercialisation.

articles.title: Nigerian fintech startup Nomba secures $3m debt facility to scale cross-border payments - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian payments startup Nomba has secured a US$3 million debt facility to scale its cross-border business from US$480 million to US$1 billion monthly, starting with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), followed by Zambia and Uganda.
Founded by Yinka Adewale and Pelumi Aboluwarin in 2017, and formerly known as Kudi, Nomba has evolved over the years into a profitable, omnichannel payment service provider.
Across its DRC operations and Canadian-licensed money service business, Nomba – which raised a US$30 million pre-Series B funding round in 2023 – processes more than US$480 million a month, and it is now aiming to scale that to US$1 billion and beyond after securing further capital.
The US$3 million debt facility, obtained through CardinalStone Finance Company Limited, will be used to expand Nomba’s cross-border payments infrastructure out of the DRC, its base for settling trade between Central Africa and Asia. The funding provides Nomba with greater USD liquidity needed to power its near-instant cross-border payment network.
“African businesses are trading more with the rest of the world every year, but the infrastructure to support that trade is still catching up. This facility gives us more room to move—more liquidity, more corridors, faster settlement. It’s also a strong signal of confidence in what we’re building for the next generation of African businesses,” said Adewale.
“We plan to keep scaling our cross-border infrastructure this year, expanding into new African markets and deepening the payment links between Africa and its trading partners in Asia.”
Ayoola Adeola, MD of CardinalStone Finance, said he was pleased to have structured the debt facility to support Nomba’s expansion.
“This transaction reflects our confidence in the growth opportunity presented by cross-border payments, and the role innovative financial infrastructure can play in connecting African businesses to global markets,” Adeola said.

articles.title: La Volkswagen ID. Polo déjà victime de son succès, « Elle a largement dépassé les prévisions initiales » - Numerama
articles.text:
La promesse d’une citadine 100 % électrique signée Volkswagen, disponible sous la barre des 25 000 €, a immédiatement fait mouche auprès des automobilistes européens. Selon des révélations d’Automobilwoche le 7 septembre 2026, le constructeur fait déjà face à une demande qui dépasse largement ses capacités de production initiales.
La Volkswagen ID. Polo a dépassé les 30 000 commandes depuis la présentation du 29 avril, alors même que les clients n’ont pas encore pu tester le modèle. Et la France n’est pas en reste.
5 000 commandes en France, mais l’Allemagne championne
Le succès se confirme très concrètement dans l’Hexagone : Volkswagen France nous confirme avoir clôturé le mois d’août avec près de 5 000 commandes enregistrées pour l’ID. Polo. Pour donner un ordre de grandeur, la marque a immatriculé 6 087 ID.3 sur les huit premiers mois de l’année en France (hors nouvelle version ID.3 Neo).
À l’échelle de l’Europe, la dynamique est encore plus forte. Un porte-parole de la marque a confirmé à Automobilwoche que l’ID. Polo a « largement dépassé les prévisions initiales, notamment en Allemagne ». Le directeur d’un important concessionnaire Volkswagen allemand a expliqué : « Toute la gamme ID. Polo est épuisée. Le délai d’attente est d’au moins dix mois. »
Une très bonne nouvelle pour le constructeur, un peu moins pour les clients qui voient les délais de livraison s’allonger pour les véhicules configurés individuellement. La marque a prévu un peu de stock de véhicules préconfigurés pour les clients les plus pressés.
Tout repose désormais sur l’usine de Martorell (Espagne) qui va devoir rapidement s’adapter à la demande. Le porte-parole de Volkswagen a précisé : « La forte demande de nos clients et les capacités de production planifiées à long terme de notre usine de Martorell entraînent actuellement des délais de livraison plus longs. » Il confirme par ailleurs que les délais seront réduits au fur et à mesure de la montée en cadence du site.
Skoda Epiq et Cupra Raval : la triplette MEB+ fait carton plein
La déferlante ne se limite pas à Volkswagen. Skoda pourrait même une nouvelle fois voler la vedette à la maison mère. Le petit SUV tchèque Skoda Epiq, dont le lancement officiel intervient fin septembre, comptabilise déjà plus de 35 000 commandes en Europe selon Automobilwoche.
La Cupra Raval affiche elle aussi une rupture de stock sur plusieurs mois, avec des livraisons renvoyées au printemps prochain.
« Ce sont les voitures que le marché attendait », résume un distributeur du groupe, soulignant que dans un contexte économique difficile, les clients se ruent sur des véhicules électriques aux tarifs enfin réalistes. Avec ce trio d’attaque sous la barre symbolique des 26 000 €, le groupe Volkswagen tient enfin son levier principal pour démocratiser l’électrique en Europe.
Le Volkswagen ID. Cross devrait lui aussi contribuer à ce succès du constructeur allemand un peu plus tard dans l’année. Cela devrait bien bouger pendant les prochains mois dans les classements des voitures électriques en Europe.
